power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Cholera is considered a paradigm for climate-sensitive diseases, yet its relation with El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the dominant mode of interannual climate variability, remains poorly quantified in Africa where most cholera deaths occur.

Using 15 years of surveillance data across 30 African countries and novel statistical and simulation frameworks, we identify five geographically coherent ENSO-cholera teleconnection groups, each characterized by distinct directions, strengths and timing of effects on outbreak occurrence, duration and incidence.
For the unfolding major El Niño of 2026-27, we project two-to five-fold greater cholera burden in Eastern and Horn of Africa than under ENSO-neutral conditions.
These findings identify immediate priorities for anticipatory action and establish a dynamic framework for attributing burden for outbreak-prone diseases to climate variability.
Intensifying interannual climate variability linked to anthropogenic global warming poses major challenges for societal wellbeing and public health (1) (2) (3).

text.text: Cholera exemplifies this challenge.
The ongoing seventh cholera pandemic kills far more than the roughly 7,000 deaths reported to the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2025, with the great majority of deaths in Africa (12).

text.text: Yet Africa is also where ENSO effects on cholera remain most poorly understood.

Despite its reputation as a model climate-sensitive diseasehttps://paperpile.com/c/NmaHPX/GnMb+sSYv+jR96 frequently invoked in the public health and climate change literature, the quantitative basis for cholera's climate sensitivity is thin: rigorous evidence beyond the seminal studies linking cholera dynamics to ENSO in South Asia is scarce (13) (14) (15) , and the evidence available for Africa does not provide testable predictions on how the timing and magnitude of a specific El Niño event affect cholera burden (16).

text.text: ENSO's influence may also depend on the outbreak phase: the climatic conditions that allow outbreaks to ignite are not necessarily the same as those that sustain transmission or determine its final size.

Previous insights about this phenomenon were forestalled by limited availability of high-resolution cholera surveillance data at continental scale and the lack of analytical frameworks providing information on when, how and where ENSO matters most for igniting and fueling cholera outbreaks.
Public health planning has thus been contained to qualitative intuitions to guide anticipatory action without a quantitative evidence base of ENSO-driven cholera risk.

Closing this evidence gap is particularly urgent against the backdrop of the major El Niño predicted to reach record-breaking levels in 2026-27 (22) https://paperpile.com/c/NmaHPX/uKya and governments and international agencies that are actively seeking preemptive approaches to limit cholera risk (23).

text.text: Here we leverage a unique 15-year surveillance database spanning 30 African countries to unravel the ENSO-cholera relationship using a Bayesian hierarchical framework that jointly estimates the direction, strength, and timing of ENSO effects on outbreak initiation, duration, and incidence at subnational scale, pooling information across the continent.
We identify geographically coherent ENSO-cholera teleconnection groups, and assess the role of past major ENSO events on cholera burden in different regions of Africa.
We finally turn these inferences into testable, region-specific forecasts for the unfolding 2026-27 El Niño event, identifying where anticipatory action may have the highest impact.

Our raw dataset consisted of 2,442 unique cholera outbreaks of at least 50 suspected cholera cases at subnational level, extracted following established methods from weekly and sub-weekly incidence time series spanning 2010 to 2024 and 1,400 unique locations in 30 countries in Africa (materials and methods; figs. Our results demonstrate that during strong El Niño events (ONI at +1.5), outbreaks are twice as frequent in GH and GE, and 50% more frequent in GS (occurrence Incidence Rate Ratio [oIRR], GH: 2.3, 95% Credible Interval [CrI]: 1.1-4.2; GE: 2.1, 95% CrI: 1.1-3.9; GS: 1.5, 95% CrI: 0.9-2.4), with no statistically significant differences in duration (cessation IRR [cIRR], GH: 1.5, 95% CrI: 0.8-2.8; GE: 0.9, 95% CrI: 0.6-1.5; GS: 0.8, 95% CrI: 0.5-1.3) or incidence (monthly suspected case IRR [mIRR], GH: 1.1, 95% CrI: 0.6-1.9; GS: 1.1, 95% CrI: 0.7-1.8; GE: 1.5, 95% CrI: 0.95-2.2).

El Niño has the opposite effect in GW (Western Africa excluding Nigeria plus Somalia), with around 60% lower onset risk (oIRR: 0.4, 95% CrI: 0.2-0.7), although the outbreaks that do occur tend to have 30% higher incidence rates (mIRR: 1.3, 95% CrI: 0.9-1.9); GG has a damped outbreak response.

Strong La Niña (ONI at -1.5) had effects in the same direction as strong El Niño in GH and GS, although weaker (oIRR, GH: 1.8, 95% CrI: 1.0-3.2; GS: 1.3, 95% CrI: 0.8-2.2), with longer outbreaks in GS (cIRR: 0.6, 95% CrI: 0.35-0.95), while effects were close to null in GE (oIRR: 1.3, 95% CrI: 0.7-2.3; cIRR: 0.9, 95% CrI: 0.5-1.4; mIRR: 1.4, 95% CrI: 0.9-2.1).
In GW, strong La Niña did not reduce outbreak onsets (oIRR: 0.9, 95% CrI: 0.5-1.5), but outbreaks tended to be more severe (mIRR: 1.4, 95% CrI: 0.96-2.0).

To quantify how ENSO timing and strength affect key cholera outbreak dimensions, we developed a novel stochastic disease-agnostic outbreak simulation framework that tackles the persistent question of how to attribute changes in disease burden to climatic events like El Niño and La Niña.
The simulator ingests the posterior distributions of our statistical models along with historical ONI data to produce cholera outbreak simulations (materials and methods).

Using modern filtering methods for coupled dynamical systems (30) https://paperpile.com/c/NmaHPX/liQw we reconstruct with high fidelity the historical time series of cholera outbreak states and incident cases across the continent (fig. 3a; figs.

text.text: With over 170,000 suspected cholera cases projected across Africa through October 2027 and nearly half attributable to this year's El Niño, the pressure on already-stretched global resources is acute.
Oral cholera vaccine shortages forced the WHO to permit single-dose, as opposed to standard two-dose, campaigns in 2022 to extend population reach.
While supply has since partially recovered, the scale of this projected ENSO-driven risk will likely test the stockpile and other control resources again (32).
text.formatted: While supply has since partially recovered, the scale of this projected ENSO-driven risk will likely test the stockpile and other control resources again <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, thoughtful targeting can be achieved, as our results on the geography of ENSO-driven risk point to regions where El Niño anticipatory action has the largest expected benefit.

Prepositioning or earmarking limited resources like vaccines for countries in Eastern Africa should be a strong priority for late 2026, especially since ENSO precedes outbreak onsets by 0 (GE) to 10 months (GH).

Further, enhancing the readiness to detect and respond to outbreaks in Western Africa and Somalia is critical, as this region may experience fewer outbreaks with higher incidence rates for those that do occur.
Available data in Western Africa (GW) as of September 2026 strongly align with our ENSO-informed predictions, although with different levels of agreement at the country level (fig. S26).

The analysis has three parts (fig. S1).
text.formatted: The analysis has three parts (fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">S1</ref>).

text.text: First, we extracted cholera outbreaks from sub-national surveillance records, mapped them to administrative units and built three analysis datasets, one each for outbreak occurrence, duration and monthly incidence (Section S1.1).

Second, we grouped countries by their response to the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) with a latent-class model, and fitted for each ENSO group three Bayesian hierarchical models of outbreak occurrence, duration and monthly case counts, each at an ENSO lag selected by cross-validation (Sections S1.2 to S1.5).

Third, we used the fitted models in a stochastic simulator: a particle filter reconstructs the outbreak state of every unit up to August 2026, and forward runs under factual and counterfactual ENSO conditions attribute outbreaks to past ENSO events and to the current ENSO forecast, with hindcasts to assess forecast skill (Section S1.6).

We used outbreak data from the Global Cholera Taxonomy Database, a curated compilation of suspected cholera surveillance reports [36].
text.formatted: We used outbreak data from the Global Cholera Taxonomy Database, a curated compilation of suspected cholera surveillance reports <ref type="bibr">[36]</ref>.

text.text: Each record gives the number of suspected cases, and where available confirmed cases and deaths, over a reporting interval in a reporting geography.
We call a reporting geography a location period: a named area with a fixed boundary over a given period.

We retrieved records for all countries of the World Health Organization (WHO) African and Eastern Mediterranean regions with reporting intervals between January 2010 and December 2024, together with the boundary of every location period.
We complemented the sub-national database with three national WHO sources.
The first is the annual cholera report of the Weekly Epidemiological Record (WER), which gives country totals of suspected cases for 2010-2024 [37].
text.formatted: The first is the annual cholera report of the Weekly Epidemiological Record (WER), which gives country totals of suspected cases for 2010-2024 <ref type="bibr">[37]</ref>.

text.text: The second is the WHO global cholera dashboard [38], which gives weekly national counts of suspected cases from January 2023 and national annual totals for 2023-2024.
text.formatted: The second is the WHO global cholera dashboard <ref type="bibr">[38]</ref>, which gives weekly national counts of suspected cases from January 2023 and national annual totals for 2023-2024.

text.text: The third is the WHO multi-country cholera situation reports [39], which give cumulative year-to-date national totals.
text.formatted: The third is the WHO multi-country cholera situation reports <ref type="bibr">[39]</ref>, which give cumulative year-to-date national totals.

text.text: We used these sources in two ways.
First, annual country totals identify country-years in which an outbreak cannot have occurred (Section S1.1.8).
For 2023-2024 we took the larger of the WER and dashboard totals where both report.
Second, we built a monthly national series of suspected cases.
Weeks without a report are gaps, and only complete months are retained.

Where the dashboard has no weekly report but consecutive situation reports give year-to-date totals at intervals of at most 45 days, we differenced the two cumulative totals and allocated the difference to the months of the interval between them.
A month is read as without cases when WHO reports an explicit zero over the last 28 days.
An unchanged cumulative total is read as a month without cases only for Tanzania, whose Ministry of Health declared the end of its national cholera outbreak in February 2026.
The resulting monthly national series, complete from January 2023 to August 2026 with partial counts for September 2026, is released as GitHub data folder, file D36 who national monthly.
These national-level observations enter the historical reconstruction as a country-level observation (Section S1.6.8).
We identified outbreaks building on the operational outbreak definition of Zheng et al. [36], which we applied to each country separately.
text.formatted: We identified outbreaks building on the operational outbreak definition of Zheng et al. <ref type="bibr">[36]</ref>, which we applied to each country separately.

text.text: In short, an outbreak in a location is a period of weekly incidence above the location's mean weekly incidence that totals at least 50 suspected cases.
We retained weekly and sub-weekly records at national to third administrative level, and removed records without a suspected case count.
Sub-weekly records were aggregated to weeks, and duplicate records for the same location and week were averaged.

Following our previous approach [36], we set weeks without a record within a location's series to zero suspected cases, treating an unreported week as a week without cases, and extended each series by eight zero weeks before its first and after its last record.
text.formatted: Following our previous approach <ref type="bibr">[36]</ref>, we set weeks without a record within a location's series to zero suspected cases, treating an unreported week as a week without cases, and extended each series by eight zero weeks before its first and after its last record.

text.text: Each location period was assigned the population inside its boundary from constrained 100 m WorldPop grids [25] for the median year of its records.
text.formatted: Each location period was assigned the population inside its boundary from constrained 100 m WorldPop grids <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> for the median year of its records.

text.text: The grids cover 2015-2030.

For a year outside that range we used the nearest available year, rescaled by the change in the national total of the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 (WPP) [40] while holding sub-national shares fixed.
text.formatted: For a year outside that range we used the nearest available year, rescaled by the change in the national total of the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 (WPP) <ref type="bibr">[40]</ref> while holding sub-national shares fixed.

text.text: We rescaled gridded totals to the national WPP totals unless the rescaling factor fell outside 0.5-2.
We define the outbreak threshold of a location as the mean weekly incidence, in suspected cases per person, over its whole zero-filled series.
A week is above threshold when its incidence is at least the threshold and at least one case was reported.
An outbreak starts at the first of two consecutive above-threshold weeks, and ends at the last week before a run of six consecutive below-threshold weeks.
The closing run decides that the outbreak is over but is not part of it, so episode end dates, durations and case totals exclude it.
Two starts that are not separated by such a run belong to the same outbreak, and an outbreak without a closing run lasts until the end of the series.
Finally, we discarded outbreaks with fewer than 50 suspected cases in total.
An example of the outbreak definition is shown in fig. S2.

text.text: Outbreak extraction, worked example.
Weekly suspected-cholera incidence of one location period, on a dummy series simulated for this figure (156 weeks, population 250,000; not surveillance data).
Weeks without a record are zero, and eight zero weeks pad both ends of the series.

The outbreak threshold (dashed red line) is the mean weekly incidence over the whole zero-filled series; weeks at or above it with at least one case (dark bars) are above threshold, the others (light bars) below.

An outbreak starts at the first of two consecutive above-threshold weeks and ends at the last week before six consecutive below-threshold weeks; that closing run (grey) decides the end but is excluded from the outbreak's dates, duration and case total.
A run of fewer than six below-threshold weeks inside an outbreak does not end it, so the two waves of the second outbreak form one outbreak, and a single above-threshold week does not start one.
Outbreaks with fewer than 50 suspected cases in total are discarded (orange): the two-week cluster in the middle of the series meets the start rule but stays below the 50-case floor.
We call an episode the record of one outbreak in one reporting geography: its start date, its end date and its suspected cases by month.
We then aggregate these into one episode per administrative unit and cholera year (Section S1.1.7).
We allocated case counts to calendar months by splitting the cases of each weekly record across the calendar months it overlaps.
Location periods rarely coincide with a single administrative unit.
We therefore intersected each location period with first-and second-level administrative units from the GADM database [24].
text.formatted: We therefore intersected each location period with first-and second-level administrative units from the GADM database <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Throughout, a unit is a GADM administrative unit.
We computed the population of each intersection from the same WorldPop surface.

We write H[l, g] for the population living in the intersection of location period l and GADM unit g, P l for the population of l, and Q g for the population of g, and define two shares: (share of g's population covered by l).
We discarded intersections holding less than one person or less than 0.01% of P l , renormalising the weights w lg.
We derived the administrative level at which each location period is represented from its geometry.
We first identified the best-covering level, and accepted a level one step coarser when it lost little coverage, using a coverage floor of 80% and a tolerance of 10%.
We define the dominant coverage of a location period as max g w lg , the share of its population living in its most populous unit, and call a location period composite when this is below 0.90.
We excluded composite location periods from all analyses (55 of the 1,407 location periods with an extracted outbreak, 3.9%; fig. S3), and assigned every other location period to its dominant unit.
text.formatted: We excluded composite location periods from all analyses (55 of the 1,407 location periods with an extracted outbreak, 3.9%; fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S3</ref>), and assigned every other location period to its dominant unit.

text.text: Population denominators in the models are unit populations by year from the same WorldPop surface and WPP rescaling, with the same nearest-year rule outside 2015-2030.
Cholera transmission in much of Africa follows an annual cycle whose phase varies by location [29].
text.formatted: Cholera transmission in much of Africa follows an annual cycle whose phase varies by location <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: We accounted for this seasonality by assigning each location period a trough month, the calendar month of lowest mean seasonal transmission in Perez-Saez et al. [29].
text.formatted: We accounted for this seasonality by assigning each location period a trough month, the calendar month of lowest mean seasonal transmission in Perez-Saez et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: We matched estimates at the location's own unit, then at its first-level unit, and then at the nearest unit of the same country, and set the trough month to January for location periods without any match (57 of the 2,435 sub-national location-period episodes, before the exclusions of Section S1.1.7).
Each administrative unit then receives a single calendar, given by the most frequent trough month among the location periods reporting on it.

We then define each unit's cholera year as running from trough to trough, and label a cholera year by the calendar year in which it starts, so that episodes of early 2010 can belong to cholera year 2009.
A unit can be reported on by several location periods at once, for example by a district and a province report, or by successive versions of a boundary.
We therefore aggregate location-period episodes into one episode per unit and cholera year.
The episode starts at the earliest member start and ends at the latest member end.
Its size is the total at the finest reporting level, choosing the level with the largest total, so that cases reported at two levels are not counted twice.
A unit therefore has at most one onset per cholera year.
We define the months at risk of a unit as the months covered by the surveillance series of at least one location period reporting on it.
National-level records are removed before aggregation, together with later outbreaks of a location period in the same cholera year and composite location periods (fig. S3).
text.formatted: National-level records are removed before aggregation, together with later outbreaks of a location period in the same cholera year and composite location periods (fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S3</ref>).

S3, tables S1 and S2, figs. S4 and S5).

text.text: Data processing cascade.
Records, outbreaks and episodes retained by each processing step, from the weekly records of the Global Cholera Taxonomy Database to the three analysis datasets (Sections S1.1.3 to S1.1.8).

Side boxes give what leaves the cascade at a step: records outside the WHO African and Eastern Mediterranean regions; location-period episodes outside Africa; national-level location periods; and, before consolidation, national-level location-period episodes and those without a population estimate, later outbreaks of a location period in the same cholera year (left out of the occurrence dataset) and the episodes of the composite location periods.

One mapped location period loses all its episodes at the step that removes national-level episodes and those without a population estimate, so the composite location periods are counted out of one fewer location period than are mapped.

The cascade ends in canonical outbreak episodes and forks into the occurrence, duration and monthly case-count datasets, whose counts are those of the prepared datasets, before the duration and monthly models drop first-level episodes that overlap a second-level episode.
Onsets that fall inside a running episode of an earlier cholera year of the same unit are not occurrence events, but their episodes remain in the duration and monthly datasets.

We derived three datasets from the episode dataset, one for each of the three dimensions of a cholera outbreak: when it starts (onset timing), how long it lasts (duration) and how many cases it produces each month (monthly incidence rate).
The occurrence dataset has one observation per unit and calendar month while the unit is at risk, with an onset indicator as outcome and the number of days at risk in the month as exposure.
It includes every second-level unit with at least one recorded episode in 2010-2024, and the first-level units with no reporting second-level unit.
Units without a recorded episode never enter the dataset or the simulations (fig. S5).
text.formatted: Units without a recorded episode never enter the dataset or the simulations (fig. <ref type="figure">S5</ref>).

text.text: As months at risk follow sub-national surveillance coverage, a country-month without an active sub-national series contributes nothing, even when national surveillance (Section S1.1.2) shows that the country had no cholera.
We therefore added national-zero months, country-months in which the whole country had no suspected cholera, as no-onset unit-months for every unit of the country.

We used national-level data (Section S1.1.2) to impute zeros, accounting for both monthly-level national zeros when available and annual-level observations of fewer than 60 cases (the outbreak definition limit plus 20% tolerance), as well as our subnational data.
Country-years in which WHO reported fewer than 60 suspected cases also qualify, with two edge guards.

The last four months of such a year are claimed only if the next year is also below the threshold, and the first four months only if the previous year is also below it or has no WHO figure, so that an epidemic counted by WHO but not recorded in the database cannot run into a zero January to April.
A WHO year whose database episode cases exceed 1.2 times the WHO total is treated as under-reported, and its months are not claimed unless they rest on the national series alone.
Ethiopia 2010-2016, whose WHO figures reflect reporting of acute watery diarrhoea rather than an absence of cholera, is excluded [41].
text.formatted: Ethiopia 2010-2016, whose WHO figures reflect reporting of acute watery diarrhoea rather than an absence of cholera, is excluded <ref type="bibr">[41]</ref>.

text.text: The window ends in December 2024, the last complete WHO annual-report year, and a national-zero month is never added inside a recorded episode of its unit.
This adds 12,535 unit-months without onset (17.6% of the 71,063 unit-months of the occurrence dataset).

We exclude data under the following conditions: (i) a unit is not at risk during the remaining months of an outbreak that began in an earlier cholera year; an onset recorded in those months is an episode for the duration and monthly models but not an occurrence event; (ii) where a first-level unit and its second-level units both report, the first-level unit-months are dropped, and the months of the second-level units inside a first-level episode with no overlapping second-level episode are censored, so that these units are not left at risk during a first-level outbreak; (iii) later onsets of the same location period in the same cholera year; (iv) re-dating duplicates; and (v) members absorbed into a canonical episode.
Exclusion counts by country are given in GitHub data folder, file D31 occ panel exclusions.

Over all countries, 61 onsets and 856 unit-months were removed from the risk set inside running episodes, and 670 second-level unit-months were censored under 96 first-level episodes without an overlapping second-level episode.

The duration dataset has one observation per episode and calendar month while the episode is active, with an indicator that the episode ended in that month as outcome and the number of active days in the month, floored at one day, as exposure.
We consider episodes that end within 73 days of the end of their reporting series as right-censored: 31 days, plus the six weeks of the closing run, which is not part of the outbreak.
This applies to 104 of the 1,404 episodes (7.4%).
The monthly case-count dataset uses the same episode-months, with the number of suspected cases in the month as outcome and the unit population multiplied by the number of active days as exposure.
Months without a report within an episode count as zero cases.

As in the occurrence dataset, the duration and monthly models drop the 323 first-level episodes that overlap a second-level episode, and are fitted to the remaining 1,081 episodes and 5,273 episode-months.
Tables S1 to S3 describe the canonical episodes of the analysis set without a model.

text.text: They group countries by World Health Organization African Region (WHO-AFRO) subregion: Western, Central, Eastern and Southern Africa.
Somalia and Sudan, members of the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region, are placed in Eastern Africa.

Each episode also takes the ENSO state of its cholera year (Section S1.1.6): the Oceanic Niño Index (Section S1.2.1) of the December-February season whose December lies in that cholera year, El Niño at or above +0.5 and La Niña at or below -0.5, with no persistence requirement.
The record spans 16 cholera years, from 2009 (Section S1.1.6).
At the continental level, outbreaks were more common during La Niña (96.  S3).
text.formatted: At the continental level, outbreaks were more common during La Niña (96.  <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: Overall, cholera outbreaks had a median cumulative attack rate of 78 cases/100,000 (interquartile range [IQR]: 30-195), and lasted 14 weeks (median, IQR: 8-24), with first-level episodes being slightly longer and with lower burden (table S2).

text.text: Overall, attack rates and duration differed across ENSO conditions (lower attack rates in El Niño and La Niña than in neutral years), but without a consistent pattern across subregions (table S3).

text.text: We measure ENSO with the official Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) of the NOAA Climate Prediction Center [42], the three-month running mean of ERSST sea-surface-temperature anomalies in the Niño 3.4 region (5°N-5°S, 120°-170°W) [43, 44].
text.formatted: We measure ENSO with the official Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) of the NOAA Climate Prediction Center <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">[42]</ref>, the three-month running mean of ERSST sea-surface-temperature anomalies in the Niño 3.4 region (5°N-5°S, 120°-170°W) <ref type="bibr">[43,</ref> <ref type="bibr">44]</ref>.

text.text: Writing ONI t for the index of the three-month season centred on calendar month t (the December-February value is assigned to January), the lagged exposures are ONI t-ℓ for candidate lags ℓ = -11, . . . , 11 months, of which lags below -8 months are not selected (Section S1.4.5).
A negative lag ℓ reads the index |ℓ| months after the outcome month.

As ENSO events develop over several months, the index after the outcome month can describe a developing event better than the index before it, and we therefore let the data choose between positive and negative lags.
Each model uses a single lag L, which we select as described in Section S1.4.5.
We summarise the selected lag of each model by its sign.

A positive lag L relates the outcome to the ONI L months earlier, so that cholera follows an event that has already developed (a following-year response, as events peak in December-February and cholera responds after the ENSO winter); a zero or negative lag (a lead) relates it to the ONI at or after the outcome, so that cholera responds as the event develops and peaks (a same-year response).
The class is assigned per model, so a group can be same-year for one outcome and following-year for another.

The statistical model aims to quantify how ENSO, at a group-specific lag, changes the rate at which outbreaks start, the rate at which they end and the number of cases they produce each month, accounting for seasonality, outbreak history, contagion and persistent differences between places.
Every model is fitted separately for each ENSO teleconnection group (Section S1.4.1).

We model outbreak occurrence, outbreak duration and monthly case counts with three Bayesian hierarchical models that share the same nested random effects, the same ENSO exposure basis and the same approach to anchoring the intercept on an empirical baseline rate.
We first describe this shared structure, then each model, the anchoring, the priors and the estimation settings.
We use one set of symbols in the three models.
Index i is an administrative unit (first-or second-level), t a calendar month, k an outbreak episode and s a posterior draw.

For a unit i, j(i) and c(i) are the first-level unit and the country containing it; for an episode k, i(k) is the unit in which it was recorded, t 0 (k) its onset month and d kt = t -t 0 (k) + 1 its age in month t. τ (t) ∈ {1, . . . , 12} is the calendar month of the year of month t, ℓ a candidate ENSO lag and L the selected one, h = 1, . . . , J indexes the columns of the ENSO spline basis, u denotes a random intercept and v a random slope.

We write a i for the empirical baseline rate of the cell (country and administrative level) containing unit i (Section S1.3.7); each model has its own baseline rate, written a occ i , a dur i and a mon i where the model is not clear from the context.
Observations of the occurrence model are unit-months (i, t); observations of the duration and monthly case-count models are episode-months (k, t).
We estimate the occurrence and duration models as Poisson mixed models fitted to a unit-month expansion of the data, the standard approach for piecewise-constant discrete-time hazard models [45, 46].
text.formatted: We estimate the occurrence and duration models as Poisson mixed models fitted to a unit-month expansion of the data, the standard approach for piecewise-constant discrete-time hazard models <ref type="bibr">[45,</ref> <ref type="bibr">46]</ref>.

text.text: For an interval (i, t) of length ∆t it days (a unit-month, or an episode-month for duration) with event indicator y it ∈ {0, 1} and a hazard λ it = exp(η it ) constant within the interval, the event probability is and we fit the log-linear Poisson form with log ∆t it as an offset.

With at most one event per interval and ∆t it the time at risk, this likelihood is proportional to the piecewise-exponential survival likelihood with right-censoring [45, 46], and it agrees with the grouped-time likelihood (S1) [47] to first order in λ it ∆t it , as monthly onset and cessation probabilities are small.
text.formatted: With at most one event per interval and ∆t it the time at risk, this likelihood is proportional to the piecewise-exponential survival likelihood with right-censoring <ref type="bibr">[45,</ref> <ref type="bibr">46]</ref>, and it agrees with the grouped-time likelihood (S1) <ref type="bibr">[47]</ref> to first order in λ it ∆t it , as monthly onset and cessation probabilities are small.

text.text: The simulator draws events from (S1) (Section S1.6.3).
All three models include nested random intercepts, with random slopes on selected covariates.

The nesting reflects the expectation that two administrative units in the same country are more alike than two units in different countries, and the random slopes that the effect of a covariate may also vary geographically.
We fit every model separately for each ENSO group.
As the group already stratifies the continent, no model includes a regional level.
The occurrence model nests random intercepts at country, first-level unit and second-level unit.

The duration and monthly case-count models, fitted like the occurrence model to first-and second-level units, nest them at country and first-level unit, with an additional second-level intercept for observations at second-level units.
We estimate random effects as mutually independent variance components.

We evaluate the ENSO exposure at a single lag L, selected for each model and ENSO group (Section S1.4.5), and model it as a smooth non-linear function of the index: where b 1 , . . . , b J are the basis functions of a natural cubic spline with J degrees of freedom, β h the population coefficients and v h,c(i) and v h,j(i) the country and first-level-unit random slopes of basis column h.
We write f ENSO for the population curve (v = 0).
The natural spline is linear beyond its boundary knots, which limits the curvature of the fitted curve at extreme ONI values.
We chose J together with the grouping, from the latent-class models with four to five degrees of freedom (Section S1.4.2); the chosen basis, J = 4, is used in all three models and all groups.
The random slopes on every basis column let the shape of the exposure-response curve vary geographically within a group.
The boundary knots are the extremes of the ONI values at lag L over the observations of the group's dataset, so the fit itself involves no extrapolation.
The simulations read index values beyond this range, chiefly in strong El Niño events, and clamp the index (Section S1.6.11).

We model outbreak occurrence with a Poisson mixed model of the form (S2) fitted to the occurrence dataset, with the baseline rate as a second offset (Section S1.3.7), µ it = ∆t it a occ i exp(η it ), and linear predictor where ϑ it is the day of the unit's cholera year on which month t starts (0 to 365; Section S1.1.6), s(•) is a cyclic cubic regression spline with eight knots, giving a smooth seasonal baseline hazard that joins continuously across the cholera-year boundary, f ENSO,i is the single-lag exposure-response function (S3) at the group-specific lag L, and u c(i) , u j(i) and u i are the nested random intercepts at country, first-level unit and second-level unit.

The coefficients of the outbreak-history and contagion terms vary by unit through random slopes: γ c(i) and β χ,c(i) = β χ + v χ,c(i) add a country slope to the population effects, and a country and a first-level-unit slope.
Time since last outbreak at the unit enters as a categorical variable with seven levels: less than one year, one to two years, and so on up to six years or more.
Units without an earlier recorded outbreak are assigned to the last level.
The categorical form allows a strongly non-linear effect, large in the first year or two and flat thereafter.
The within-unit contagion indicator χ it equals one when an outbreak episode was ongoing anywhere in the first-level unit j(i) at any time during month t -1.

We define the neighbour pressure V it (ρ) as the distance-weighted share of other first-level units of the same transmission unit with an ongoing outbreak one month earlier: where χ (1) j ′ ,t-1 is the ongoing-outbreak indicator of first-level unit j ′ in month t -1, defined as for χ, d jj ′ is the distance between the centroids of units j and j ′ , T (•) is the transmission unit, and ρ is a bandwidth that we fix at 500 km.

Transmission units are two pre-specified clusters of countries, Central-East and West, within which cholera activity is connected by movement and shared epidemic waves [48] (table S6); they are independent of the ENSO groups, which describe the climate signal rather than the spread of infection.
text.formatted: Transmission units are two pre-specified clusters of countries, Central-East and West, within which cholera activity is connected by movement and shared epidemic waves <ref type="bibr">[48]</ref> (table <ref type="table">S6</ref>); they are independent of the ENSO groups, which describe the climate signal rather than the spread of infection.

text.text: The normalising sum runs over every first-level unit of the transmission unit, including units never affected, so that the covariate is bounded between 0 and 1.
As it excludes the focal first-level unit j(i), it measures pressure from neighbours only and remains distinct from χ.
Neighbours are coupled across national borders within a transmission unit but not across transmission units, and second-level units take the value of their first-level unit.

Time since last outbreak and the within-unit contagion indicator have country random slopes, and the neighbour pressure and each of the J ENSO basis columns have country and first-level-unit random slopes.
The seasonal spline does not vary by unit.
We model outbreak duration with a Poisson cessation-hazard model of the same form (S2), fitted to the duration dataset, in which the outcome indicates that an ongoing episode ended in a given month.
Episodes enter at the first-or second-level unit in which they were recorded.
Episode k contributes one interval for each calendar month t during which it is active, and we denote this set of months by A k .

Each interval carries the indicator y kt ∈ {0, 1} that the episode ended in month t, the number of days e kt > 0 of month t during which the episode was active, floored at one day, and the episode's age d kt , which serves as the baseline clock.
text.formatted: Each interval carries the indicator y kt ∈ {0, 1} that the episode ended in month t, the number of days e kt > 0 of month t during which the episode was active, floored at one day, and the episode's age d kt , which serves as the baseline clock.

text.text: Writing ν kt for the cessation hazard, assumed constant within the month, the likelihood contribution of each interval is where a dur i(k) is the empirical baseline cessation rate (see Section S1.3.7) and log e kt enters as an offset, so that exp(η dur ) is a hazard ratio relative to that baseline.

The cessation log-hazard is where B(•) maps episode age d to one of six bands (months 1, 2 and 3 each form a band, followed by months 4-5, 6-8 and 9 or more), ψ 1 , . . . , ψ 6 are the band effects with ψ 1 ≡ 0 for identifiability, so that the intercept α carries the hazard of the first month, g dur is a seasonal term with two harmonics in the calendar month τ = τ (t) of the active month, capturing an annual and a semi-annual cycle, with four fixed effects θ 1 , . . . , θ 4 without random slopes, f ENSO,i(k) is the single-lag exposure-response function ( S3) with country and first-level-unit random slopes on its J basis columns, and u (•) are nested random intercepts at country and first-level unit, with a second-level intercept for episodes recorded at a second-level unit.
text.formatted: The cessation log-hazard is where B(•) maps episode age d to one of six bands (months 1, 2 and 3 each form a band, followed by months 4-5, 6-8 and 9 or more), ψ 1 , . . . , ψ 6 are the band effects with ψ 1 ≡ 0 for identifiability, so that the intercept α carries the hazard of the first month, g dur is a seasonal term with two harmonics in the calendar month τ = τ (t) of the active month, capturing an annual and a semi-annual cycle, with four fixed effects θ 1 , . . . , θ 4 without random slopes, f ENSO,i(k) is the single-lag exposure-response function ( <ref type="table">S3</ref>) with country and first-level-unit random slopes on its J basis columns, and u (•) are nested random intercepts at country and first-level unit, with a second-level intercept for episodes recorded at a second-level unit.

text.text: The band effects have their own prior, N (0, 1.5) (table S5).
text.formatted: The band effects have their own prior, N (0, 1.5) (table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: As for the occurrence model, this Poisson likelihood is the survival likelihood with right-censoring [45, 46]: censored episodes contribute months in which the cessation indicator is zero and no terminating month.
text.formatted: As for the occurrence model, this Poisson likelihood is the survival likelihood with right-censoring <ref type="bibr">[45,</ref> <ref type="bibr">46]</ref>: censored episodes contribute months in which the cessation indicator is zero and no terminating month.

text.text: The forward simulator draws cessation events from the monthly probability 1 -exp(-ν kt e kt ) (Section S1.6.4).

We model the monthly case count C kt of episode k in month t with a negative binomial mixed model: where e kt is the number of active days as in the duration model, a mon i(k) the empirical baseline rate of the episode's unit, and ζ a population elasticity on the log population log pop i(k) , centred within administrative level.
Population thus enters both as an offset and through ζ, so that case counts need not scale proportionally with population.
The seasonal term g mon has the two-harmonic form (S8) of g dur , with its own coefficients.

The within-episode epidemic curve f MSO,c is a cubic B-spline with four degrees of freedom in the episode's age d kt (months since onset), with country random slopes on its four columns, and f ENSO,i(k) is the single-lag exposure-response function (S3) with country and first-level-unit random slopes.
Random intercepts are nested at country and first-level unit, and observations at second-level units have an additional second-level intercept.
We also model the negative binomial dispersion hierarchically, with country and first-level-unit random intercepts on log ϕ i(k) .
This allows overdispersion to vary by geography, as excess variability in reported case counts reflects local surveillance practice as much as local epidemiology.
In all three models the conditional mean is a product of offsets and an exponentiated linear predictor, µ = ( n O n ) exp(η).
We include in each model an additional offset, the empirical baseline rate a, whose denominator equals the product of the model's other offsets:
The intercept then measures the log ratio of the fitted rate to the observed baseline rate, a dimensionless quantity of order one, so that exp(α) ≈ 1 is the appropriate prior centre in every model.
The numerator and denominator of a are:

Numerator Denominator (= product of the analysis's other offsets) Occurrence number of onsets days at risk Duration number of episode terminations active days (minimum one) Monthly case counts rounded monthly case count population × active days We estimate baseline rates in cells defined by country and administrative level.
For cell m with numerator total Y m and denominator total E m , the raw estimate is log(Y m /E m ).

Under Y m ∼ Poisson(E m a m ), the delta-method variance of log(Y m /E m ) is 1/Y m , and we shrink each cell towards its country parent, the rate of its country pooled over administrative levels after adjustment to a common level (below), with the empirical-Bayes weight ), where ξ 2 is the between-cell variance in excess of Poisson sampling noise, which we estimate by moments over cells with at least one event as ξ2 = var(log âm ) -mean(1/Y m ), floored at 10 -6.
Baseline rates also differ systematically by administrative level, as a finer unit has a smaller population and therefore a different event rate per unit time.

We estimate this difference between levels within countries (the level contrast), and use it to adjust a cell to a common level before pooling it into a coarser parent and to re-express a borrowed parent rate at the target level.

The contrast is the level coefficient of a Poisson regression of the numerator on administrative level and country with the log denominator as offset, in which the country term performs the demeaning.
A contrast whose confidence interval includes zero is set to zero.

We resolve the rate of each cell in order of specificity: (i) for a cell with observations, its own shrunken estimate, which for a cell without events is its country parent; (ii) for a cell without observations in a country observed only at other administrative levels, that country's rate adjusted to the target level; (iii) the ENSO-group rate; and (iv) the continent-wide rate.
No cell needed (iii) or (iv).

Of the 60 country-by-level cells at the first and second administrative levels, 51 have observations of their own in the occurrence model, 51 in the monthly model and 46 in the duration model, in which 5 further cells have observations but no termination and take the value of their parent.
The remaining 9 cells borrow a level-adjusted country rate.

In the duration model the between-cell variance is at its floor, indicating no heterogeneity in cessation rates beyond Poisson noise once country and level are accounted for; the shrinkage weights are then close to zero, and every duration cell takes, in effect, the rate of its country parent.
All three models retain a second-level contrast.
We compute one baseline-rate table for the whole continent, used by every group and model and by the simulator.
Table S5 lists the priors.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S5</ref> lists the priors.

text.text: The intercept α has a normal prior, and every fixed-effect coefficient β, including the ENSO basis coefficients, a normal prior centred at zero.

The standard deviations of random intercepts and slopes at the country and administrative-unit levels, the smoothing standard deviation of the seasonal spline and the random-effect standard deviation of the log dispersion have half-normal priors.

In the single-country group GG (Nigeria), the country-level random effects are kept, so that the simulator draws them like those of the other groups, under a tight N + (0, 0.05) prior on their standard deviations, as one country cannot inform a between-country variance.
As the intercept measures a log ratio to the empirical baseline rate, its prior puts 95% probability on fitted rates within roughly a factor of seven of the observed baseline rate.

The prior on the other fixed effects (all but the duration band effects, whose prior is wider; table S5) puts 95% probability within roughly a factor of 2.7 per unit change in a covariate on the rate scale.
text.formatted: The prior on the other fixed effects (all but the duration band effects, whose prior is wider; table <ref type="table">S5</ref>) puts 95% probability within roughly a factor of 2.7 per unit change in a covariate on the rate scale.

text.text: We chose the random-effect standard deviation priors based on prior-predictive simulations, which showed that wider scales imply between-unit rate ratios of implausible magnitude.

For the seasonal spline of the occurrence model we used N + (0, 0.35) on the smoothing standard deviation, as the heavy-tailed half-t 3 prior with scale 2.5 allows seasonal amplitudes far larger than observed and dominated the residual prior-predictive over-prediction even with the intercept anchored.

We fitted all models with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo as implemented in the Stan programming language [49], with four chains of 350 warm-up and 1,000 sampling iterations, giving 4,000 posterior draws per model.
text.formatted: We fitted all models with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo as implemented in the Stan programming language <ref type="bibr">[49]</ref>, with four chains of 350 warm-up and 1,000 sampling iterations, giving 4,000 posterior draws per model.

text.text: We assessed convergence for every model using the potential scale reduction factor R, bulk and tail effective sample sizes, the number of divergent transitions after warm-up, and the energy-based Bayesian fraction of missing information (GitHub data folder, file D27 convergence, fig. S11).
text.formatted: We assessed convergence for every model using the potential scale reduction factor R, bulk and tail effective sample sizes, the number of divergent transitions after warm-up, and the energy-based Bayesian fraction of missing information (GitHub data folder, file D27 convergence, fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">S11</ref>).

text.text: Two structural choices are made from the data: which countries share an ENSO exposure-response (the grouping) and at which lag the index enters each model.

Both encode the timing and sign of the ENSO teleconnection, which differ across Africa and are not known a priori precisely enough to fix per country, so we make both by predictive comparison, in two steps.

We first estimate the partition of countries with a latent-class extension of the occurrence model, in which every class has its own ENSO lag and exposureresponse curve, choosing the number of classes and the spline basis from a country-block cross-validation comparison and the agreement of the chains (Section S1.4.2).
Within this partition, we then select the lag of each model and group by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation over the lag grid, with L ≥ -8 (Section S1.4.5).
The class lags of the latent-class model only define the partition.
As the same occurrence data choose the partition and fit the group models, we report each country's membership uncertainty beside its effects.
The influence of ENSO on African rainfall and temperature differs in sign, strength and timing between regions [20].
text.formatted: The influence of ENSO on African rainfall and temperature differs in sign, strength and timing between regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: We therefore fitted every model separately for each of five ENSO groups of the 30 countries with outbreak data (table S7, fig. S6a).
text.formatted: We therefore fitted every model separately for each of five ENSO groups of the 30 countries with outbreak data (table <ref type="table">S7</ref>, fig. <ref type="figure">S6a</ref>).

text.text: The groups are data-informed: they are the classes of a latent-class model of outbreak occurrence, in which countries that share an ENSO lag and exposure-response form one class (Section S1.4).
They are classes of countries, not necessarily contiguous geographic regions.
We name each group after the part of the continent in which most of its members lie, and list them from west to east and south: GW (West), GG (Guinean Gulf), GH (Horn), GE (East) and GS (South).
GG holds Nigeria alone; most other countries of the Gulf of Guinea coast are in GW.
Table S7 lists the members of each group.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S7</ref> lists the members of each group.

text.text: Released data files label each group by the a priori regional group whose seed countries fix its class, which keeps the class labels identifiable (Section S1.4.2; table S7).
text.formatted: Released data files label each group by the a priori regional group whose seed countries fix its class, which keeps the class labels identifiable (Section S1.4.2; table <ref type="table">S7</ref>).

text.text: In the latent-class model each country c belongs to one of K classes q = 1, . . . , K, and the ENSO term of a unit-month (i, t) of a country in class q is a Gaussian kernel over the lag grid centred at the class lag µ q , with a fixed width σ ω = 1.5 months and a uniform prior on µ q over [-11, 11], applied to a natural cubic spline of the index with J degrees of freedom.
text.formatted: In the latent-class model each country c belongs to one of K classes q = 1, . . . , K, and the ENSO term of a unit-month (i, t) of a country in class q is a Gaussian kernel over the lag grid centred at the class lag µ q , with a fixed width σ ω = 1.5 months and a uniform prior on µ q over <ref type="bibr">[-11, 11]</ref>, applied to a natural cubic spline of the index with J degrees of freedom.

text.text: The rest of the linear predictor is that of the occurrence model (S4) without a regional level, and the class coefficients β (q) have country and first-level-unit random slopes.

Class membership is marginalised at country level: the likelihood of a country is the mixture over classes of the likelihood of all its unit-months, with membership probabilities softmax q (log π q + κA cq ), where A is the one-hot encoding of an a priori partition into East Africa, the Horn of Africa, Southern Africa, West Africa and Nigeria (table S7) and κ ≥ 0, with a half-normal prior, measures how strongly the data retain it.
text.formatted: Class membership is marginalised at country level: the likelihood of a country is the mixture over classes of the likelihood of all its unit-months, with membership probabilities softmax q (log π q + κA cq ), where A is the one-hot encoding of an a priori partition into East Africa, the Horn of Africa, Southern Africa, West Africa and Nigeria (table <ref type="table">S7</ref>) and κ ≥ 0, with a half-normal prior, measures how strongly the data retain it.

text.text: Classes are identified by a core of seed countries fixed to their a priori group (Tanzania, Uganda and Burundi; Ethiopia and Sudan; Malawi, Zimbabwe and Zambia; Niger, Liberia and Togo; Nigeria).
The seeds identify the classes: without them the mixture is unchanged by a relabelling of its classes, and in exploratory fits the chains swapped class labels or left classes empty.
Fixing a core of countries to each class keeps the labels fixed within a chain, so that chains can be compared and averaged class by class.

The core of each of the four regional classes is made of the countries that fell in the class of their a priori group in about 85% or more of the chains of exploratory four-class fits seeded with one country per class, which had left some classes with a single member; Uganda and Burundi are fixed with Tanzania, and Nigeria, its own a priori group, seeds the fifth class alone.
All other countries are free.

We fitted the model over a grid of natural-spline bases with four to five degrees of freedom and two to five classes, with a priori partitions for fewer than five classes that merge whole groups of the five-group partition, and compared the fits by country-block approximate leave-one-out cross-validation, one block per country (table S8).

text.text: Each fit ran eight chains of 400 warm-up and 300 sampling iterations.

The latent-class model is multimodal, so we also required the chains of a fit to agree: we retained the three chains whose class lags agree best (the smallest maximum difference between their class lags), and summarised every fit on these chains.
A mode is a set of chains whose class lags agree within 1.5 months; the mode sizes of every fit are given in table S8.
text.formatted: A mode is a set of chains whose class lags agree within 1.5 months; the mode sizes of every fit are given in table <ref type="table">S8</ref>.

text.text: We selected the final fit, with four degrees of freedom and K = 5 classes, because its three agreeing chains form its dominant mode and its difference in expected log predictive density to the best fit of the comparison, -16.4 (standard error 14.2), is about one standard error.
The best fit, with five degrees of freedom and five classes, has no mode of three chains.
Each country is assigned to its class of highest mean posterior membership probability over the agreeing chains, and we write p max for that probability.
Fig. S6c shows how the classes change as K rises from 2 to 4 at the selected basis, and panel b the final fit with K = 5.

text.text: We describe each class by the final groups of its members: a class written GW + GG holds the countries of both groups, and "part of" gives the share of a group's countries that the class holds.

The most probable classes are, at K = 2: GW + GG + GH, GE + GS; at K = 3: part of GW (10 of 15) + GH + GS, part of GW (5 of 15) + GG, GE; at K = 4: part of GW (10 of 15) + GS, part of GW (5 of 15) + GG, GH, GE; at K = 5: GW, GG, GH, GE, GS.
The final partition keeps part of the regional structure of the a priori partition, and two of the 30 countries are assigned to a class other than the one their a priori group seeds (table S7).

text.text: Panel c of Fig. 1 in the main text outlines the main rainy season or seasons of each teleconnection group.
text.formatted: Panel c of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> in the main text outlines the main rainy season or seasons of each teleconnection group.

text.text: For each first-level administrative unit we computed the monthly rainfall climatology, the mean CHIRPS rainfall [50] of each calendar month over 1990-2019, from the admin-level climate dataset of the VIMC climate project [51] (for units without their own series, the mean over their second-level units).
text.formatted: For each first-level administrative unit we computed the monthly rainfall climatology, the mean CHIRPS rainfall <ref type="bibr">[50]</ref> of each calendar month over 1990-2019, from the admin-level climate dataset of the VIMC climate project <ref type="bibr">[51]</ref> (for units without their own series, the mean over their second-level units).

text.text: A calendar month is rainy in a unit when its climatological rainfall exceeds the unit's average month, one twelfth of its annual total [52]; units receiving less than 100 mm a year have no rainy season.
text.formatted: A calendar month is rainy in a unit when its climatological rainfall exceeds the unit's average month, one twelfth of its annual total <ref type="bibr">[52]</ref>; units receiving less than 100 mm a year have no rainy season.

text.text: A month belongs to a group's main season when at least half of the group's 2025 population, from the population estimates described in Section S1.1.5, lives in units in which that month is rainy.
Weighting by population rather than counting units prevents sparsely populated arid units from shaping a group's season.
Each run of consecutive such months, allowed to cross the year end, is outlined as one season, so a group with two rainy seasons shows two outlines.
Months close to the 50% threshold could fall on either side of it under a different population year or climatology period.

We compared the rainy seasons of Section S1.4.3 with the monthly pattern of each outcome, by ENSO group and calendar month (the fitted seasonal patterns are shown in panel c of Fig. 1 in the main text).
text.formatted: We compared the rainy seasons of Section S1.4.3 with the monthly pattern of each outcome, by ENSO group and calendar month (the fitted seasonal patterns are shown in panel c of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> in the main text).

text.text: For occurrence we computed the number of outbreak onsets per 1,000 unit-months at risk in the occurrence dataset, by the calendar month of the onset.
For cessation we computed the number of episodes ending per 100 active episode-months in the duration dataset.
For case counts we took the median and interquartile range of suspected cases per active episode-month in the monthly dataset, leaving out months with a reporting gap.
All three are computed on the units the models are fitted to (Section S1.1.8).
Onset and cessation rates carry exact Poisson 95% intervals.
A month with fewer than five events is not used to locate a peak.
Observed onsets peak in a rainy-season month in all five groups, cessation in one of the five groups and cases per active month in three of the five groups.

Once the country partition was established, for each model and ENSO group, we fitted the single-lag model (S3) separately at every candidate lag L ∈ {-11, . . . , 11} months, and compared the fits by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation with Pareto-smoothed importance sampling [53].
text.formatted: Once the country partition was established, for each model and ENSO group, we fitted the single-lag model (S3) separately at every candidate lag L ∈ {-11, . . . , 11} months, and compared the fits by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation with Pareto-smoothed importance sampling <ref type="bibr">[53]</ref>.

text.text: For each lag we computed the expected log pointwise predictive density relative to the best lag, together with the standard error of the paired difference.
A negative lag is admissible because the index after the outcome month is a function of the developing ENSO event, which can precede its own peak by several months.
We select for each model and group the lag with the highest expected log predictive density among the lags allowed by a floor, L ≥ -8.

The floor keeps the index a model reads within the forecast's reach: the firm forecast horizon of a group is the last month of the ENSO forecast plus its smallest lag (Section S1.6.12), so a lag of -9 to -11 months would end it within a few months of the launch.
The duration and monthly case-count lags are selected independently of the occurrence lag.
Selected lags are given in table S9, and full rankings, with the Pareto k diagnostics of every lag, in the GitHub data folder, file D7 lag loo ranking and fig. S7.
text.formatted: Selected lags are given in table <ref type="table">S9</ref>, and full rankings, with the Pareto k diagnostics of every lag, in the GitHub data folder, file D7 lag loo ranking and fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_9">S7</ref>.

text.text: We call two lags distinguishable only when their difference exceeds two standard errors of the paired difference; the rankings give, for every model and group, the number of lags within two standard errors of the best, and in several of them the selected lag is a point choice among nearly equivalent lags.
The floor binds in three of the 15 combinations of model and group (duration model of GH, best lag -9; monthly case-count model of GH, best lag -10; monthly case-count model of GG, best lag -11).

Table S9 reports for every model and group the floor, whether the best lag lies below it and the paired difference in expected log predictive density that this costs, the second-best lag and the best non-negative lag, each with its difference to the best lag.

text.text: We reconstruct posterior exposure-response curves draw by draw.

For each posterior draw s, we combine the fitted basis coefficients β (s) 1 , . . . , β (s) J with the spline basis evaluated on a grid of ONI values, and express the result as an incidence rate ratio relative to the reference ONI0 = 0, the centre of ENSO-neutral conditions:
We summarise curves by the pointwise median and the equal-tailed 50% and 95% credible intervals of IRR (s) (ONI) across draws.
Group-level curves use the fixed-effect coefficients, and country-and first-levelunit curves add the corresponding random slopes to β
For an ENSO state ONI 1 ∈ {-1.5, -1, 1, 1.5, 2}, a first-level unit has an effect of magnitude m in a model when its unit-level rate ratio (S13) at ONI 1 lies above 1 + m or below 1/(1 + m).
The effect is adverse when it means more cholera: onset and case rate ratios above 1 + m, and a cessation hazard ratio below 1/(1 + m), hence longer outbreaks.
It is protective in the opposite direction, and we also count effects in either direction.
We evaluate magnitudes m ∈ {0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50} and posterior probability cut-offs p ∈ {0.5, 0.8, 0.95}, for each of the three models alone and for any of them.

A unit is counted at (m, p) when the model, taken on its own, gives a posterior probability of at least p to an effect of magnitude m in the chosen direction; for "any model", when at least one of the three models does.
The headline count is the population of the units with an adverse effect in any of the three models at m = 0.25 and p = 0.95.

It is complemented by the expected population with an effect, the posterior mean and 95% interval over draws of the population of the units whose drawn rate ratio lies beyond the same bound, and by the counts at every other magnitude, cut-off and direction (data S1, files D10 enso exposure exceedance and D12 enso exposure by country).
Populations are the 2025 estimates of each unit of the dataset (Section S1.1.5).
We use the fitted models to simulate outbreak histories forward in time under factual and counterfactual ENSO trajectories.
This section describes the simulator, the particle filter that reconstructs the historical state, and the hindcast, forecast and attribution designs.
