The simulator is a discrete-time Markov chain with state at the end of month t
All other quantities needed by the models at month t + 1 are deterministic functions of S t and of the exogenous covariates.
As the models were fitted to recorded episodes, the contagion covariates and the time since last outbreak are built from detected rather than latent activity.

Each simulated episode is detected at onset with probability 1 -δ fn and keeps this status while it lasts, and an inactive unit records a false alarm with monthly probability δ fp , with δ fn and δ fp as in the measurement model of Section S1.6.8; A d it = 1 for a detected episode or a false alarm.
We compute the two contagion covariates from the detected indicators as where is the detected state of first-level unit j and w is the distance kernel of (S5), restricted to the transmission unit.
As in the fitted model, χ includes the unit's own activity and V excludes it.
In the fitted data, the neighbour covariate counts recorded activity only, so a neighbour without surveillance in the previous month counts as inactive.
We measured this coverage without changing the covariate.

A unit was under surveillance in a month if one of its location periods had a reporting window covering it (including first-level series), the month was a national-zero month, or the unit had a recorded episode then.
For each unit-month we computed the kernel-weighted share of its neighbours under surveillance in the previous month, over the same kernel and transmission-unit restriction as the covariate.

In the simulations every unit is simulated, so the implicit coverage there is one, and the simulator applies the contagion effect at a neighbour activity that the fit may not have observed where coverage was low.
Coverage by country, group and year is given in GitHub data folder, file D33 contagion coverage.

Time since last outbreak advances at each month without a detected onset, and resets at a detected onset; false alarms feed the contagion covariates but do not reset it: where we advance the counter by the mean month length δ rather than by the calendar length n t , as it only feeds a coarse categorical coding.
A unit with no recorded onset is coded in the oldest category (six years or more), as in the fitted model.
Months since onset advance while an episode is active and are undefined otherwise.

The within-year clock of the seasonal baseline hazard resets at each location's trough month, but the state variables do not: recent outbreak history and ongoing outbreaks carry over across the cholera-year boundary in calendar time.

As the distance kernel is zero between transmission units (Section S1.3.4), no state variable couples them: transmission units evolve independently given a posterior draw and the covariates, and are simulated in parallel.
Each holds 15 modelled countries of several ENSO groups (table S6).
text.formatted: Each holds 15 modelled countries of several ENSO groups (table <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: Each country is simulated with the models, selected lags and posterior draws of its own ENSO group, while the contagion terms couple it to its neighbours.
At each month, we evaluate the occurrence model for every unit not currently experiencing an episode, given the current state and the covariates: where it is given by (S4) evaluated at draw s.
Following (S1), the probability of an onset during the month is

The simulator follows the fitted risk set, from which a unit leaves after an onset until the next cholera year (Section S1.1.7): the hazard (S16) is that of the first onset of a cholera year, so we draw an onset only for a unit that is inactive and has had no detected onset yet in its current cholera year.

With τ cy it ∈ {0, . . . , 11} the month of the unit's cholera year, counted from its first month, this holds when U it / δ ≥ τ cy it , U it being read before its update (S15), or when the unit has no detected onset at all.

A unit whose episode ends within the cholera year is therefore not at risk again before the next one, and simulated detected onsets, like the fitted data and the observations the hindcasts are scored against, number at most one per unit and cholera year.
An undetected episode does not close the risk set, as an unrecorded episode does not in the fitted data.

For an episode k active at (i, t) with D it months since onset, we evaluate the cessation hazard from the duration model at draw s, where η dur,(s) it is given by (S7) with its band term evaluated at the simulated episode age D it and its seasonal term at the calendar month of t.
The episode ends during the month with probability q (s) where e it is the number of days of month t during which the episode is active.

As the simulator does not resolve days within a month, it sets e it to the length of the month, halved in the onset month (the expected active fraction under a uniformly distributed day of onset) and, in the case-count step (S21), also halved in the month the episode ends, whose cessation is drawn before the case count, as in the fitted dataset, where an episode's first and last months are partial.
The cessation probability itself carries only the onset correction, as whether the month is the last is what it draws.

Episode durations therefore follow a discrete-time survival distribution, in which the probability that an episode starting in month t 0 is still active after d months is and the expected duration in months is E[D] = d≥0 P (D > d).
text.formatted: Episode durations therefore follow a discrete-time survival distribution, in which the probability that an episode starting in month t 0 is still active after d months is and the expected duration in months is E[D] = d≥0 P (D > d).

text.text: As the cessation hazard combines a categorical function of months since onset with the calendar-month harmonics (see Section S1.3.5), (S20) reproduces the non-geometric empirical distribution of durations, in which few episodes end in their first month and the monthly probability of ending levels off from the third, and the expected duration depends on the month of onset.

For each month in which an episode is active, we draw a case count from the monthly model, where η(s) it collects the non-offset terms of (S10) (intercept, population elasticity, seasonality, within-episode curve, ENSO and random effects) evaluated at draw s, with the within-episode curve f MSO evaluated at the simulated D it .
The negative binomial is parametrised such that Var(C) = µ + µ 2 /ϕ.
The mean and the drawn count are both capped at 15% of the unit's population per month.

In the simulator and the historical reconstruction, the population pop it of a unit is resolved for every simulated month at that month's cholera year, the calendar year of the month m i -1 months before t, with m i the unit's trough month (see Section S1.1.6).
This is the convention under which the monthly case-count model was fitted.
Populations come from the unit population table (2015-2030), and years outside it are rescaled by the national totals of the UN World Population Prospects 2024.
The population offset, the population elasticity term and the incidence cap therefore follow population growth over the simulated period.

Per-capita rates (annualised incidence and attributable cases per 100,000) divide by the month-weighted mean population over the months each estimate covers, and counts of people living in affected areas use the 2025 population.
We simulate each replicate r independently for each transmission unit, such that replicate-unit pairs can be distributed across processors.

Each replicate uses a single posterior draw s r for all three models of every ENSO group in the transmission unit, so that occurrence, duration and case-count parameters come from a coherent posterior state.
The initial state S 0 is a terminal state of the particle filter (see Section S1.6.8).
At each month t = 1, . . . , M , we compute the covariates x it and the contagion covariates from S t-1 using (S14).

We then draw onsets with (S17) for units in the risk set (Section S1.6.3), cessation for active units with (S19), and case counts for units active during the month with (S21), and update A, A d , D and U to obtain S t .
Each replicate returns its event table, with the onset month, duration and total cases of every episode, and its unit-by-month state array.
Detection only feeds the covariates.
Every reported simulated quantity, in the reconstruction, the hindcasts, the forecasts and the attribution, counts latent onsets and cases, detected or not.
Random number streams are seeded by replicate, so results do not depend on parallelisation.

With Y (r) it and C (r) it the onsets and cases of replicate r and R the number of replicates (Section S1.6.7), the marginal onset probability at (i, t) it , and the expected total number of cases R -1 r t C (r) it , with credible intervals given by empirical quantiles across replicates.
For a scalar summary Z of a simulated trajectory, for instance the total number of outbreaks in a country over a horizon, the total variance decomposes as
Replicates at a fixed posterior draw resolve the first term, and replicates across posterior draws the second.
The forward simulations nest replicates within draws in a fixed cycle: replicate r runs posterior draw s r = ((r -1) mod S) + 1 of a fixed set of S draws, so that every draw is run by R/S replicates.

The forecast, the counterfactual, the attribution factual and the past-event arms run R = 10,000 replicates per transmission unit and arm, S = 100 draws of R/S = 100 replicates each (GitHub data folder, file D34 run design), and the factual and counterfactual arms of a replicate share its draw.
The hindcasts run 5,000 replicates per run in the same cycle, 50 replicates per draw.
Intervals over replicates reflect the sum (S22); the intervals of the attributable fraction separate the second term (Section S1.6.14).
Forecasts and counterfactuals require a starting state consistent with the observed record.

We therefore reconstruct the latent state of the simulator over the observed record, from January 2011 to August 2026, by sequential Monte Carlo before any forward simulation, with the sub-national database as observation to December 2024 and the WHO monthly national series from January 2023 to August 2026.
The reconstruction ends in the last month with a published ONI season, so that the forecasts start from the latest observed ENSO state.
The ENSO covariates of the reconstruction are the observed ONI throughout; for models with a negative lag, the months after August 2026 are taken from the calibrated ENSO forecast described below.

We write X t = (X 1t , . . . , X It ) for the latent state of all units at month t, where X it comprises the active and detected-activity indicators, the months since onset, the time since last outbreak and the current case-count mean.
The transition density f (X t | X t-1 ; θ (s) ) is the one-step simulator described above, evaluated at a fixed posterior draw.
The observations at (i, t) are the reported onset indicator Ỹit and, where available, the reported case count Cit.
As reporting is imperfect, we allow for false negatives, onsets that are not recorded, with probability δ fn , and false positives, recorded onsets without a latent onset, with probability δ fp .
The onset term of the measurement model is where Y it is the latent onset indicator.

The term is evaluated in the unit-months of the occurrence dataset; that dataset, with the months removed inside running episodes and its national-zero months (Section S1.1.8), sets the risk set of the filter.
The case term is evaluated in every unit-month with a recorded count, including months after an onset, with zeros recorded in at-risk months without a case report.
Writing µ it and ϕ i for the mean and dispersion of the monthly model, it is where A it is the latent active indicator.

In an inactive unit a count is reported with probability ε, drawn from a negative binomial with a floor mean µ0 = 0.1, so that the term is a probability distribution over the reported count in both states.
The first case penalises latent episodes that continue through months without recorded cases, and the fourth particles whose episode has ended while cases are still reported.
We set ε = 1, so that the inactive term is the floor negative binomial at every count; ε cannot be estimated, as every at-risk month outside the recorded episodes is recorded as zero.
Missing observations do not contribute to the likelihood.
We set δ fn = 0.10 and δ fp = 0.001, reflecting the assumption that under-ascertainment is possible and that spurious outbreak reports are rare.
The WHO monthly national series enters as a third, country-level term.

Writing W ct for the national count of country c in month t and C sim ct = i:c(i)=c C it for the particle's simulated cases summed over the modelled units of the country, the term is where w c is a country multiplier and ϕ W = 5 is a reporting overdispersion distinct from the dispersion of the monthly model, as the process variation is already in C sim .
With φ c the share of the national population living in the modelled units of the country, the multiplier is by default w c = 1/φ c , which scales the simulated count to the national total.

Where WHO and the database both observe a country over enough months in 2023-2024 (at least 100 database cases over at least 6 overlap months), we estimate its own scale instead: with W c the WHO total and DB c the database total over the simulated units in those months, ς c = W c φ c /DB c , clamped to [0.1, 10], and w c = ς c /φ c , which equals W c /DB c unless clamped.
This identified 2 of 30 countries; the others keep the fixed factor 1/φ c (GitHub data folder, file D30 who scale).
To avoid scoring a country-month twice, the WHO count is not scored in country-months the database observes.
The floor mean of one case gives a particle without simulated activity in the country a finite, graded penalty when cases are reported.
This term is evaluated from January 2023; from January 2025, after the end of the sub-national database, it is the only observation, and countries without WHO data run unconstrained from then on.
Scoring the simulated count rather than its expectation lets the filter also condition on the sampling variation of the case-count model.

We use the block particle filter [54, 55] implemented in the spatPomp package [30], with one block per country, so that the national term enters its block exactly once, one independent filter run per transmission unit, 30,000 particles, 100 replicates and a 24-month burn-in (January 2009 to December 2010) before the filtering window.
text.formatted: We use the block particle filter <ref type="bibr">[54,</ref> <ref type="bibr">55]</ref> implemented in the spatPomp package <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>, with one block per country, so that the national term enters its block exactly once, one independent filter run per transmission unit, 30,000 particles, 100 replicates and a 24-month burn-in (January 2009 to December 2010) before the filtering window.

text.text: Smoothing replicate j runs the filter at draw j of the 100 posterior draws in every transmission unit, and returns one state path over the whole record.

At the last month, the filter samples one particle per block and traces its ancestry back in time, so that the path is a draw from the smoothing distribution, stitched across the countries of the transmission unit, and its state in any month is conditioned on the whole record, later months included.
We call these paths the historical reconstruction.
Their last states are the initial states S 0 of the forecasts; the hindcasts and the past-event arms start from an earlier month of the same paths.

Forward replicate r starts from the state of smoothing replicate s r (Section S1.6.7), one smoothing replicate per posterior draw, and runs the draw s r under which that state was reconstructed, so that state and parameters are a joint posterior draw.
The pairing depends only on the replicate number, and is the same in every transmission unit and arm.
We compare simulated and observed outbreak histories over their common period, restricted to unit-months with documented surveillance coverage.
The same scores serve the hindcasts (Section S1.6.10).

We assess the calibration of the binary monthly onset outcome with the randomised probability integral transform for discrete outcomes [56], which is uniform on (0, 1) when the predictive distribution is calibrated.
text.formatted: We assess the calibration of the binary monthly onset outcome with the randomised probability integral transform for discrete outcomes <ref type="bibr">[56]</ref>, which is uniform on (0, 1) when the predictive distribution is calibrated.

text.text: A U-shaped histogram indicates under-dispersed predictions, a hump-shaped one over-dispersed predictions, and a sloped one a systematic bias.

We measure predictive accuracy for onset counts and case totals with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) [57], estimated from the simulated ensemble with the fair estimator, which does not favour ensembles of a particular size [58].
text.formatted: We measure predictive accuracy for onset counts and case totals with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) <ref type="bibr">[57]</ref>, estimated from the simulated ensemble with the fair estimator, which does not favour ensembles of a particular size <ref type="bibr">[58]</ref>.

text.text: Lower scores are better, and the score rewards sharpness subject to calibration.

We also perform four structural checks comparing simulated and observed month-of-year onset frequencies across the modelled units, the distribution of episode durations, the fraction of unit-months in the active state, and the probability of an onset given an ongoing outbreak in the previous month in the same first-level unit, in another first-level unit of the same country, or in another country of the same transmission unit (fig. S15).

S16 and S17.
We assess retrospective forecast skill with hindcasts.
The hindcast years lie inside the fitting period, and the grouping, the lags and the parameters were estimated with them, whereas the reference forecasts leave the scored season out (below).

Each hindcast also starts from the historical reconstruction, which has seen the observations of the season it scores (Section S1.6.8), and it reads the observed ENSO index over the scored season rather than a forecast available at launch.

The scores are therefore in-sample upper bounds on the skill of the model given perfect knowledge of ENSO; they check consistency and do not establish the skill of a forecast issued in real time (Section S2.1).
Hindcasts follow the cholera season of each country, from trough to trough.

A country's trough is the calendar month with the lowest onset rate (onsets per at-risk unit-month, three-month circular smoothing) in the occurrence dataset over 2010-2024, where the country has at least 30 onsets and the trough is stable (within one month in at least 80% of 500 year-bootstrap resamples), and otherwise the trough month shared by most of its units in the cholera-season calendar (Section S1.1.6).
This trough, estimated from the onsets themselves, can differ from the calendar trough that sets the cholera years of the models and the past-event windows.
The season window runs from the month after the trough to the next trough month inclusive, one month later than a cholera year that starts at the same trough.
Its start is floored at May, after the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the months cut by the floor and their share of onsets are reported (GitHub data folder, file D3 season ends).

Each country is scored to the end of its season window, extended by the smallest of the three selected lags of its group when that lag is positive; the past-event windows are extended by the largest of the three instead (Section S1.6.16).
For each cholera year from 2012 to 2022, we run one hindcast per transmission unit and launch month.

These are the first and last cholera years that fit entirely inside the January 2010 to December 2024 data window with their margins: the launch state needs the reconstructed months and the lagged ONI before it, and the season window, extended by the lag, must close before the data end.

In each run, the countries whose season starts in that month are launched together from the state of the preceding month in the historical reconstruction, the whole transmission unit is simulated, and only those countries are scored in that run.
The observed ONI is used both over the window and in the months before launch that enter its initial state.
We score occurrence on the number of onsets per unit over each season window, in units and months at risk.

Its reference is a climatology of the unit itself: a binomial distribution over the unit's at-risk months in the window, with the unit's own onset rate over its at-risk months outside the scored season, so that the scored season does not enter its own reference; its CRPS is computed exactly.

We score case counts per month and per season total on the at-risk units, against a pooled monthly climatology: for each scored month, the cases of the same calendar month and its two neighbours in the other cholera years, leaving out the scored season and every season overlapping it, scaled to the population of the scored year.
The model ensemble is scored with the fair CRPS (Section S1.6.9) on raw counts and on log(1 + y), and with a threshold-weighted CRPS that counts errors above the 50-case outbreak threshold.
Skill is CRPSS = 1 -CRPS/ CRPS ref , with both sums over the same units, months and seasons, pooled by ENSO group, for Africa and by country.

Leads count from each country's own launch and are grouped into early (0-3 months), peak-season (4-8; labelled "peak" in the figures, not to be confused with the peak of an ENSO event) and late (9 or more) classes.
Intervals come from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of whole cholera years (figs.
S18 and S19).
Fig. S19a shows the skill against the two climatologies by ENSO group and lead class, for onsets and for monthly case counts on both scales.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">S19a</ref> shows the skill against the two climatologies by ENSO group and lead class, for onsets and for monthly case counts on both scales.

text.text: The hindcasts tend to over-predict case totals: the observed total of a group window (one ENSO group and launch year) falls below the 95% prediction interval in 11 of the 55 group windows and above it in two (fig. S19b).

text.text: Forecasts start in September 2026 from the filtered state at the end of the observed record (August 2026), with the replicates and draws of the forward arms (Section S1.6.7).
This is the forecast shown in the figures; the attribution statistics use a second factual arm launched with the counterfactual (Section S1.6.13).

Over the forecast horizon, we draw the ENSO input from the 40 member trajectories of the latest NCEP Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2) monthly Niño 3.4 forecast issued by the NOAA Climate Prediction

Beyond the last month whose ONI is a full three-month CFSv2 mean (the month before the last CFSv2 target month), each replicate's trajectory is continued with an analogue drawn from unforced climate-model simulations.

We built a library from the Niño 3.4 series of the pre-industrial control runs published with Lenssen et al. [65] (CMIP6 and earlier NMME and CMIP5-generation models), each rescaled to the standard deviation of the observed ONI over 1991-2020, and characterised every month of every run by its calendar month, its ONI, its three-month tendency and its ONI six months earlier.
text.formatted: We built a library from the Niño 3.4 series of the pre-industrial control runs published with Lenssen et al. <ref type="bibr">[65]</ref> (CMIP6 and earlier NMME and CMIP5-generation models), each rescaled to the standard deviation of the observed ONI over 1991-2020, and characterised every month of every run by its calendar month, its ONI, its three-month tendency and its ONI six months earlier.

text.text: For a replicate whose CFSv2 trajectory ends in state (v, ∆v, v -6 ), we took the library months of the same calendar month, ranked them by the standardised Euclidean distance over these three features, keeping at most one start per two years within a run, and drew one of the 30 nearest.
The continuation follows the analogue's subsequent months, with the offset between the replicate's last value and the analogue's start fading with a three-month time constant.

In a validation on 468 observed seams between 1982 and 2020, this continuation scored better (fair CRPS 0.22, 0.40 and 0.43 at leads of 1-6, 7-12 and 13-24 months) than persistence with autoregressive decay (0.44, 0.75, 0.80), climatology (0.47, 0.47, 0.46) and a neutral continuation (0.67, 0.66, 0.65).

One run (GFDL CM2.1-NMME) was excluded from the library because it is the longest run, supplying a third of the starts, and has the strongest cold bias after strong El Niño events; its exclusion improved the score after such events from 0.42 to 0.38 at leads of 7-12 months.
The library therefore holds 10 runs, and the same runs supply the counterfactual analogues (Section S1.6.13).
A forward simulation covers every month from its launch to the end of its horizon, both included, and starts from the reconstructed state of the month before the launch.

As each model uses ENSO at its selected lag, a group's firm horizon is the last month whose ONI is a full three-month CFSv2 mean plus the smallest lag selected for that group across the three models; with a negative lag it falls before that month, and a group whose firm horizon equals the launch month keeps one firm month (table S9, fig. S21, GitHub data folder, file D6 firm horizons).
text.formatted: As each model uses ENSO at its selected lag, a group's firm horizon is the last month whose ONI is a full three-month CFSv2 mean plus the smallest lag selected for that group across the three models; with a negative lag it falls before that month, and a group whose firm horizon equals the launch month keeps one firm month (table <ref type="table">S9</ref>, fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S21</ref>, GitHub data folder, file D6 firm horizons).

text.text: Months past a group's firm horizon read the analogue continuation of ENSO.
A transmission unit mixes ENSO groups and is simulated to the latest firm horizon among its countries, with the analogue continuation supplying the ENSO input where needed.
Summaries by group, and the country panels of figs.
S22 and S23, censor each country at the firm horizon of its own group; the attribution of the 2026 forecast reads every group over one calendar window for Africa (see Section S1.6.13).
Each replicate thus combines one ENSO trajectory, one posterior draw and one filtered terminal state.

In the counterfactual arm we replace the ENSO trajectory over the forecast horizon with trajectories of unforced internal ENSO variability, drawn from the pre-industrial control archive of Lenssen et al. [65].
text.formatted: In the counterfactual arm we replace the ENSO trajectory over the forecast horizon with trajectories of unforced internal ENSO variability, drawn from the pre-industrial control archive of Lenssen et al. <ref type="bibr">[65]</ref>.

text.text: With the neutral analogue set of the main analysis, the difference between factual and counterfactual forecasts gives the cholera outbreak burden attributable to the observed and forecast ENSO state relative to ENSO-neutral conditions; with the full pool of analogues, it is the burden relative to unforced internal ENSO variability of either sign (below).

The counterfactual trajectories are anchored in May 2026, the last month before the 2026-27 El Niño developed, and the counterfactual arm is launched from the filtered state at the end of April 2026, so that the counterfactual ENSO departs from the observed ONI in the same month in which the epidemic state is released from the observations.

Every attribution statistic compares this arm with an attribution factual: the factual arm launched from the same end-of-April state, with the same smoothing replicate, random number seed and posterior draw for each replicate, so that the two arms differ only in their ENSO trajectory.
The forecast shown in the figures is a third arm, launched from the August 2026 state, which retains the national counts observed from May to August 2026; it enters no attributable quantity.

The difference between the displayed forecast and the counterfactual decomposes per posterior draw into an ENSO component (attribution factual minus counterfactual) and an information component (displayed forecast minus attribution factual), the latter being the effect of the months observed between the two launches (GitHub data folder, files D22 attrib information scope and D22 attrib information decomposition).

The end-of-April state is itself a smoothed state, reconstructed from observations to August 2026, so the information component compares the realised May to August record with its re-simulation, not with a forecast made in April.
The counterfactual analogues come from the same library as the factual continuation (Section S1.6.12), with the same rescaling, features and excluded run.

From the last observed month before the launch, we select the 100 analogues per model nearest in ONI level, three-month tendency and ONI six months earlier, standardised by the library's feature standard deviations and at least 12 months apart within a model, over 10 models.

Each path is joined to the observed ONI of the launch month, with the offset between analogue and observation decaying with an e-folding time of three months, so that both arms start from the observed ONI and differ only through the analogues' evolution.

We classify every December to February (DJF) winter read by a reported month (the month minus the group's ENSO lag) on the mean of the monthly ONI over December to February, with thresholds of -0.5 and +0.5 °C and no persistence requirement.

A trajectory belongs to the La Niña, neutral or El Niño set if its first winter has that phase and every later winter it reads is neutral; otherwise it is labelled mixed and kept only in the full pool.

For the 2026 forecast, the pool of 1,000 trajectories gives 30 La Niña, 151 neutral and 208 El Niño analogues; set sizes, model shares, seam errors and the mean ONI of every classified winter are given in GitHub data folder, files D29 analog sets, D29 analog sets winters and D29 analog sets models.

The main analysis draws counterfactuals from the neutral set, which asks what the coming season would hold without an ENSO event of either sign; the full pool and the two other conditional sets are reported in the supplementary figures.

We write N F r and N C r for a burden summary, either the number of outbreaks or total cases, under the factual and counterfactual arms in replicate r, using the same posterior draw and random number stream in both arms, and report two estimands.
The first is the ratio of expectations, which we map on a log 10 scale.

We use the ratio of expectations rather than the expectation of ratios because most administrative units have no outbreak in most replicates, so that per-replicate ratios are mostly undefined or infinite.

The second is the paired difference, which is defined in every replicate and provides the uncertainty statement: we report a shift as credible when a central interval of the empirical distribution of {∆ r } excludes zero.
Pairing removes the stochastic and parameter variation shared by the two arms, such that Var[∆] is much smaller than Var[N F ] + Var[N C ].
Probability-of-increase maps are not paired.
Results for each analogue set are shown in figs. S24 and S25, and the forecast and neutral-ENSO counterfactual of each country in figs. S22 and S23.
text.formatted: Results for each analogue set are shown in figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_20">S24</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S25</ref>, and the forecast and neutral-ENSO counterfactual of each country in figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_18">S22</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_19">S23</ref>.

text.text: The attribution covers one calendar window for every ENSO group, from the attribution start to October 2027 (the firm horizon of group GS, ENSO lag +4 in the occurrence model), and summaries for Africa as a whole sum the groups over that window.

Groups whose firm horizon ends earlier are read on into the analogue continuation of ENSO, both arms alike, and groups forecast further are cut at the window end; GitHub data folder, file D23 africa scope gives each group's longest continuation lead per model and the skill of the analogue continuation against climatology at that lead.
The counterfactual constrains every winter read by the reported months to be neutral.
We summarise the paired factual and counterfactual simulations with five metrics, each answering a different question.
All are computed from the same replicates, per first-level administrative unit and for each country, ENSO group and Africa as a whole.
For a first-level unit j and replicate r, N F j,r and N C j,r are the total cases or the number of outbreak onsets over the comparison window in the factual and counterfactual arms.

Scope totals sum their units within each replicate, N F z,r = j∈z N F j,r ; countries and ENSO groups use the replicates paired within their group, and Africa uses the replicates present in every group, so that no total mixes draws from different replicates.
The main results keep every replicate.

As a sensitivity analysis, a replicate pair is removed from every unit of an ENSO group (and from Africa) when, in either arm, any unit of the group reaches 2 × 10 5 cases in a month of the window or the cumulative cases of the group over the whole window reach 10 6 ; in the posterior intervals below, the pair is removed from every group of its transmission unit, so that the groups of a unit keep one set of replicates.
As this conditions on the outcome, and the factual arm reaches these thresholds more often where ENSO raises incidence, it pulls the attributable fraction towards zero.
The pairs removed because of each arm and the resulting change in the attributable fraction are given in GitHub data folder, file D24 explosive pairs.

We report two comparison windows: the main window, from the common launch in May 2026, and, as a sensitivity analysis, a window restricted to the months after the launch of the displayed forecast in September 2026.
In both, the attribution factual and the counterfactual are free simulations from the same state.
The intervals of the attributable number and fraction, and of the exposed population of the ratio-of-means rule below, are posterior intervals of the ENSO effect.

For posterior draw s, N F s and N C s are the mean window totals over the R/S replicates that ran s (Section S1.6.7), summed over the units of a scope at the same draw (the draw indexes the fit of the unit's ENSO group, so that a scope within one group sees one parameter vector), and AF s = 1 -N C s / N F s .

These per-draw means still carry the epidemic variation of their replicates, so the variance of AF s across draws overstates the posterior variance by the within-draw noise, as in a nested simulation whose inner samples are the replicates of one draw [66], or in the analysis of variance that separates internal variability from the spread between climate-model ensemble members [67].
text.formatted: These per-draw means still carry the epidemic variation of their replicates, so the variance of AF s across draws overstates the posterior variance by the within-draw noise, as in a nested simulation whose inner samples are the replicates of one draw <ref type="bibr">[66]</ref>, or in the analysis of variance that separates internal variability from the spread between climate-model ensemble members <ref type="bibr">[67]</ref>.

text.text: We write vnoise for the mean over draws of the delta-method variance of AF s , computed from the within-draw variances and covariance of the replicate totals, and vdraws for the variance of AF s across draws, so that vdrawsvnoise is the method-of-moments estimate of the posterior variance.

Rather than report that variance alone, we shrink AF s towards the pooled value by max(0, 1 -vnoise /v draws ) before taking the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles over draws; this rescaling keeps the centre and shape of the ensemble of draws and matches its variance to the estimate, the constrained Bayes estimator of a population of parameter values [68, 69], in place of the conditional-mean shrinkage that would narrow the ensemble by the full noise share.
text.formatted: Rather than report that variance alone, we shrink AF s towards the pooled value by max(0, 1 -vnoise /v draws ) before taking the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles over draws; this rescaling keeps the centre and shape of the ensemble of draws and matches its variance to the estimate, the constrained Bayes estimator of a population of parameter values <ref type="bibr">[68,</ref> <ref type="bibr">69]</ref>, in place of the conditional-mean shrinkage that would narrow the ensemble by the full noise share.

text.text: When the estimated noise share vnoise /v draws of a scope or first-level unit reaches 0.8, the replicates cannot separate its posterior spread from their epidemic variation.
We then report its pooled value with the range of its replicates and no posterior interval; the figures draw that range dashed.

The interval of the exposed population of the ratio-of-means rule covers the first-level units whose spread is identified, and the population of the others is reported separately, with the part whose pooled estimate passes the rule.

Africa is computed like an ENSO group: the replicate totals of every simulation unit are summed within each replicate before the per-draw means, so that groups simulated together in one transmission unit keep their dependence.
Draw s indexes the fit of each group and transmission units are simulated independently, so the sum at one draw index is a joint draw.

Replicate quantiles of N F r -N C r (below) describe the spread of single paired simulations, epidemic noise included; so do the cumulative window totals of the main-text forecast figure, shown as the median and 50% and 95% quantiles across paired replicates, whereas its attributable fractions are the noise-adjusted posterior intervals above.
Population counts use the 2025 population of the observed reporting units of each simulated first-level unit, and shares are of the population of the simulated first-level units in the scope.

The attributable number and fraction of cases or onsets are where N F and N C are means over replicates and RR is the ratio of expectations of eq. ( S27), so that AF coincides with the FAR of that equation.
text.formatted: The attributable number and fraction of cases or onsets are where N F and N C are means over replicates and RR is the ratio of expectations of eq. ( <ref type="table">S27</ref>), so that AF coincides with the FAR of that equation.

text.text: These are the attributable number and fraction of health impact attribution [70, 71, 72].
text.formatted: These are the attributable number and fraction of health impact attribution <ref type="bibr">[70,</ref> <ref type="bibr">71,</ref> <ref type="bibr">72]</ref>.

text.text: We also report the replicate quantiles of N F r -N C r and of (N F r -N C r )/N F r , and the attributable number per 100,000 population.

For an outbreak event E we compare its probability in the two arms, the probability ratio of event attribution [73] and the probabilities that the ENSO forecast was a necessary, a sufficient, and a necessary and sufficient cause of the event [74]; PN is the fraction of attributable risk of event attribution.
text.formatted: For an outbreak event E we compare its probability in the two arms, the probability ratio of event attribution <ref type="bibr">[73]</ref> and the probabilities that the ENSO forecast was a necessary, a sufficient, and a necessary and sufficient cause of the event <ref type="bibr">[74]</ref>; PN is the fraction of attributable risk of event attribution.

text.text: We keep the sign of PN, PS and PNS, so that negative values indicate an event made less likely.
We use two events: at least one outbreak onset in the window, and window cases of at least 50, the outbreak-size threshold of the episode database.

When no counterfactual replicate has the event while some factual replicates do, PR is infinite; we then report as lower bound p 1 /p u 0 , where p u0 = 1 -0.05 1/R is the exact one-sided 95% upper bound on p 0 given zero events in R replicates [75, 76].
text.formatted: When no counterfactual replicate has the event while some factual replicates do, PR is infinite; we then report as lower bound p 1 /p u 0 , where p u0 = 1 -0.05 1/R is the exact one-sided 95% upper bound on p 0 given zero events in R replicates <ref type="bibr">[75,</ref> <ref type="bibr">76]</ref>.

text.text: PS is undefined when p0 = 1.
In large scopes both arms almost always contain the event and PR tends to one, so we interpret the probability ratio at the first-level-unit and country level.
Population with a larger expected burden.

Following Childs et al. [72], a first-level unit counts towards the exposed population at magnitude m ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1} when its mean factual total is positive and at least (1 + m) times its mean counterfactual total; a positive factual mean against a zero counterfactual mean counts, and two zero means do not.
text.formatted: Following Childs et al. <ref type="bibr">[72]</ref>, a first-level unit counts towards the exposed population at magnitude m ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1} when its mean factual total is positive and at least (1 + m) times its mean counterfactual total; a positive factual mean against a zero counterfactual mean counts, and two zero means do not.

text.text: We report the posterior mean and 95% credible interval of this population, applying the rule to each draw's shrunk AF s , using N F ≥ (1 + m) N C ⇔ AF ≥ m/(1 + m).
We also report the rule on replicate medians, which is not driven by the few replicates with very large outbreaks; it has no interval.

Following the robustness assessment of the IPCC AR6 Atlas [77], with m as the variability threshold, a unit has a robust increase when at least 66% of the paired replicates have N F j,r > (1 + m) N C j,r and at least 80% have N F j,r > N C j,r (ties counting as disagreement), a conflicting signal when only the first condition holds, and no robust signal otherwise.
text.formatted: Following the robustness assessment of the IPCC AR6 Atlas <ref type="bibr">[77]</ref>, with m as the variability threshold, a unit has a robust increase when at least 66% of the paired replicates have N F j,r > (1 + m) N C j,r and at least 80% have N F j,r > N C j,r (ties counting as disagreement), a conflicting signal when only the first condition holds, and no robust signal otherwise.

text.text: With the paired difference ∆ r = N F r -N C r of (S28), the signal-to-noise ratio where s ∆ is the standard deviation of ∆ r across replicates, measures the change relative to the epidemic variability that remains after pairing [78].
text.formatted: With the paired difference ∆ r = N F r -N C r of (S28), the signal-to-noise ratio where s ∆ is the standard deviation of ∆ r across replicates, measures the change relative to the epidemic variability that remains after pairing <ref type="bibr">[78]</ref>.

text.text: We report the population of the units in which the signal has emerged, S/N ≥ γ for an increase, S/N ≤ -γ for a decrease, at γ = 1 and γ = 2.
Unlike the robustness classes, this measure needs no magnitude threshold; for a normally distributed difference, S/N = 1 corresponds to an increase in 84% of the replicates.

The first two metrics quantify how much burden, and how much more likely an outbreak, the forecast ENSO state implies; the last three locate the population where the expected burden is higher by a margin, where the replicates agree on the change, and where the change stands out from the epidemic noise.
For the West group we compare the modelled ENSO effect on 2026 with the WHO national counts (fig. S26).
text.formatted: For the West group we compare the modelled ENSO effect on 2026 with the WHO national counts (fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S26</ref>).

text.text: The modelled ratio is the mean of the historical reconstruction over the mean of its neutral-ENSO counterfactual, over the only months both arms cover, May to August 2026 (the counterfactual is launched from the reconstruction in May, and the reconstruction ends in August).
Each counterfactual replicate is paired with the reconstruction replicate it was launched from, and the interval is the spread of the ratio across the reconstruction replicates.

The observed ratio is the 2026 WHO count over the mean of the ENSO-neutral years since 2010, standardised to the 2026 population, with one pseudo-case on each side; a year is neutral when its mean ONI lies within ±0.5 °C. It has two estimators: the same calendar months (May to August), for which the WHO monthly series covers only the neutral years 2024 and 2025, and the 2026 year to date against full neutral years, a lower bound.
Countries without a WHO series are left out rather than counted as zero, and Somalia, whose 2026 series stops in January, is censored.

Over the countries with an observed ratio, the modelled West ratio is 7.0 (95% interval over replicates 3.9 to 14.4), against an observed 7.4 for the same months (Cameroon and Congo) and a lower bound of 7.0 for the year to date (Central African Republic, Cameroon, Congo and Chad; modelled 6.3 for these countries).

We apply the paired design of the forecast attribution to three strong ENSO events of the study period: the El Niño events of 2015-16 and 2023-24 and the La Niña of 2020-23, attributed as one event (table S10).
text.formatted: We apply the paired design of the forecast attribution to three strong ENSO events of the study period: the El Niño events of 2015-16 and 2023-24 and the La Niña of 2020-23, attributed as one event (table <ref type="table">S10</ref>).

text.text: For each event we launch both arms in the month before the ONI crossed +0.5 (El Niño) or -0.5 (La Niña) and stayed beyond it until the event's first peak: September 2014, August 2020 and May 2023.
For the 2020-23 La Niña, whose ONI returned above -0.5 in May to August 2021, this persistence applies to the first of its three winters only.

Both arms start from the reconstruction state of the month before the launch (Section S1.6.8), which has seen the observations of the event, and are paired as in the forecast: same reconstructed state, posterior draw and random number stream, with the replicates and draws of the forward arms (Section S1.6.7).
The factual arm uses the observed ONI throughout, as the hindcasts do (Section S1.6.10), but runs over the whole event window from a single launch and is not scored.

The counterfactual arm replaces the ONI from the launch month onwards with analogue trajectories from the pre-industrial control archive of Lenssen et al. [65], built as in Section S1.6.13 and joined to the observed ONI of the launch month.
text.formatted: The counterfactual arm replaces the ONI from the launch month onwards with analogue trajectories from the pre-industrial control archive of Lenssen et al. <ref type="bibr">[65]</ref>, built as in Section S1.6.13 and joined to the observed ONI of the launch month.

text.text: We draw from the neutral set, so that the counterfactual describes the seasons had the event not developed.
The ONI of the months before the launch is the observed one in both arms, and, as in the forecasts, the ONI entering each model is clamped to its widened boundary knots (Section S1.6.11).

The 2020-23 La Niña is attributed as one event: one launch (August 2020, the month before the ONI crossed -0.5), one pair of factual and counterfactual runs per transmission unit, and counterfactual analogues neutral in each of the event's three La Niña winters (DJF 2020/21, 2021/22 and 2022/23).
Later winters read by the reported months (DJF 2023/24) are not constrained.
The event's counterfactual has 83 neutral analogues.
Results are reported for the whole event and for consecutive per-winter sub-windows.
Windows are set per country.

The comparison window runs from the launch to the end of the country's cholera year containing the peak of the event (see Section S1.1.6), extended by the largest positive lag selected for its group across the three models, so that the lagged response of every model to the peak falls within the window (the hindcasts use the smallest lag instead, Section S1.6.10).

For the La Niña, the k-th sub-window ends with the cholera year containing the k-th winter's ONI peak plus the same lag, and the next sub-window starts the month after; the sub-windows partition the event window, so their attributable numbers add up to the event's, but their attributable fractions do not.
A transmission unit is simulated to the latest window end among its countries, and each country is censored at its own window end.
As windows are set per event, the later La Niña sub-windows may overlap the window of the 2023-24 El Niño, and the burdens of the two events are then not additive.
We read the factual arm in two ways.
The first is the free simulation with observed ENSO.
The second replaces, over the whole window, the factual series of replicate r with the historical reconstruction of the filtered replicate it starts from (see Section S1.6.8).

This anchors the factual arm to the observations, but it conditions that arm on data the counterfactual arm does not see, so that the contrast also contains the misfit of the model to the observations.
The two arms of this reading also treat the index differently: the reconstruction does not clamp the ONI, whereas the counterfactual arm holds it within the widened knots.
As the reconstruction has 100 replicates, this reading has at most as many distinct factual series.

From each pair of arms we derive the attributable number and fraction (S29), the probability ratio and probabilities of causation (S30), the signal-to-noise ratio (S31) and the two population metrics, as in Section S1.6.14, with every replicate kept, the same scope totals and, for the free simulation, the same posterior intervals over draws (fig. S20); the reading with the reconstruction as factual is a point estimate.
text.formatted: From each pair of arms we derive the attributable number and fraction (S29), the probability ratio and probabilities of causation (S30), the signal-to-noise ratio (S31) and the two population metrics, as in Section S1.6.14, with every replicate kept, the same scope totals and, for the free simulation, the same posterior intervals over draws (fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S20</ref>); the reading with the reconstruction as factual is a point estimate.

text.text: In the main-text figure, the bars of Africa and each ENSO group show the median of this noise-adjusted posterior with its interval, whereas the per-unit maps show the attributable fraction of the replicate means, a point value without interval.
As both arms launch in the same month, there is a single comparison window per country.

To relate the simulated fraction to the observed burden, we also report the observed-anchored attributable number 29 where Y z is the observed total of scope z over its simulated unit-months, with its interval from that of AF z and Y z held fixed.

Observed onsets are taken from the occurrence dataset and observed cases from the monthly case-count dataset, using for each unit-month the largest total among its reporting levels (see Section S1.1.7).
We report alongside the share of simulated unit-months in the occurrence dataset, as a measure of surveillance coverage, and the ratio of Y z to the mean factual total, as a check of the factual arm.
As a cross-check without epidemic dynamics, we compute the burden attributable to each event directly from the fitted models on the observed data [70].
text.formatted: As a cross-check without epidemic dynamics, we compute the burden attributable to each event directly from the fitted models on the observed data <ref type="bibr">[70]</ref>.

text.text: For an observed unit-month (i, t) in the window with outcome y it (an onset in the occurrence model, cases in the monthly case-count model), posterior draw s and a counterfactual trajectory ONI drawn for that draw from the event's neutral analogue set, where b l and L are the basis columns and selected lag of the model (S3), ONI equals the observed ONI before the launch, and β (s) l,i combines the population coefficients with the country and first-level random slopes of unit i (the country-level coefficients for a unit without a random effect).
Both ONI series are clamped to the widened knots as in the simulations.

We report the mean and 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles over 400 posterior draws of the fitted models (the simulations use 100 per model), which carry both parameter uncertainty and the spread of the counterfactual ENSO trajectories.

This calculation uses every observed unit-month of a group's countries, including reports at coarser levels that the simulations do not represent, and it ignores the effect of ENSO on contagion and on the immunity carried between seasons.
We fitted all models in R [79] using Stan [49] through the brms interface [80] and the cmdstanr backend [81].

The ENSO index, the ENSO forecasts, the pre-industrial ENSO trajectories, the population estimates and the administrative boundaries are publicly available from the sources cited in Materials and Methods.
Although our analysis builds on the most comprehensive continent-wide database of cholera, it has several limitations.
First, our data are suspected cases, with case definitions and reporting that vary between countries and over time.

Where confirmation is reported, episodes with a confirmed case have onset-rate contrasts by ENSO phase broadly consistent with those of all episodes, where the data allow the comparison (table S4), which suggests that the suspected-case signal is not driven by non-cholera diarrhoea.
text.formatted: Where confirmation is reported, episodes with a confirmed case have onset-rate contrasts by ENSO phase broadly consistent with those of all episodes, where the data allow the comparison (table <ref type="table">S4</ref>), which suggests that the suspected-case signal is not driven by non-cholera diarrhoea.

text.text: Reporting that intensifies around outbreaks independently of ENSO would tend to dilute an ENSO effect rather than create one.
Second, the ENSO teleconnection groups and the lag of each model are selected on the data the grouped models are fitted to.
The partition is the dominant mode of one of several nearly equivalent fits (Section S1.4.2), and the selected lags are often within two standard errors of others (Section S1.4.5).

Because we select the lags on a fixed partition after the grouping pass, we do not propagate the grouping uncertainty to our ENSO effect estimates, although the overall patterns were consistent across the numbers of groups we tested, despite multimodality across MCMC chains.

We also did not account for the Indian Ocean Dipole, which is known to act synergistically with ENSO on climate patterns in Africa; it could explain some of the remaining uncertainty in the ENSO effects and is a subject for further study.

Third, neither our inferential models nor our outbreak simulator account for external drivers such as conflict or displacement, nor for cholera prevention and control measures such as vaccination or water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) interventions.

There is evidence that ENSO increases the risk of conflict, so we believe that our estimates represent a total effect of ENSO through these pathways; in the occurrence model, which conditions on recorded outbreak history and contagion, they are direct effects with respect to those terms.
Reactive cholera control may have shortened outbreaks, reduced their size or prevented large outbreaks from igniting, possibly diluting the association between ENSO and cholera.

Accounting for these interventions is challenging because unified continent-level data on their implementation over the study period are scarce, but including them in future analyses would improve our estimates of how ENSO is associated with cholera outbreaks in Africa.

More technically, we use a single source of ENSO forecasts, one calibrated CFSv2 issuance, without multi-model or issuance-to-issuance uncertainty, continued past each group's firm horizon by analogues whose skill falls with the lead (Section S1.6.12).

Larger ensembles would make the ENSO forecast more robust, but we believe this uncertainty is marginal: ONI values were already high at the time of writing, and there is little doubt that 2026-27 will be a very strong El Niño event, although the peak ONI value it will reach remains uncertain.

Finally, our hindcasts are in-sample: we initialise the simulator from a smoothing state that has seen the scored season, and we use the observed ONI rather than the forecast values available when the simulation is launched.
We therefore consider the reported hindcast skill an upper bound, with real-time skill probably lower.

We nevertheless know of no other systematic quantification of seasonal cholera predictions, and the fact that these simulations outperform climatology across several regions and lead times points to a promising avenue for ENSO-or weather-informed early warning systems for cholera.

text.text: Raw CFSv2 Niño 3.4 forecasts are biased, and in strong El Niño events they overshoot the observed amplitude.

We therefore calibrate them with the probability-distribution and spread correction CPC applies operationally to CFSv2 Niño 3.4 [60], which we rebuild from the CFSv2 hindcasts because CPC publishes the corrected forecast only as a figure.
text.formatted: We therefore calibrate them with the probability-distribution and spread correction CPC applies operationally to CFSv2 Niño 3.4 <ref type="bibr">[60]</ref>, which we rebuild from the CFSv2 hindcasts because CPC publishes the corrected forecast only as a figure.

text.text: The CFSv2 hindcasts that train the correction are taken from the North American Multi-Model Ensemble archive [61], averaged over the Niño 3.4 box: 360 start months from 1991 to 2020, leads of 0 to 9 months and 24 to 28 members per start; the real-time forecast is the 40-member CPC forecast above.
text.formatted: The CFSv2 hindcasts that train the correction are taken from the North American Multi-Model Ensemble archive <ref type="bibr">[61]</ref>, averaged over the Niño 3.4 box: 360 start months from 1991 to 2020, leads of 0 to 9 months and 24 to 28 members per start; the real-time forecast is the 40-member CPC forecast above.

text.text: As in CPC's procedure, the 1991-2020 sample pools hindcasts initialised before and after the 1999 change in the CFSv2 ocean initial conditions [62, 63].
text.formatted: As in CPC's procedure, the 1991-2020 sample pools hindcasts initialised before and after the 1999 change in the CFSv2 ocean initial conditions <ref type="bibr">[62,</ref> <ref type="bibr">63]</ref>.

text.text: For initialisation month o and lead ℓ f (written ℓ in the subscripts below), let F oℓ denote the empirical distribution function of all member anomalies of these forecasts (each relative to its own start-month and lead mean) and G oℓ that of the observed Niño 3.4 anomalies in the corresponding target months.
text.formatted: For initialisation month o and lead ℓ f (written ℓ in the subscripts below), let F oℓ denote the empirical distribution function of all member anomalies of these forecasts (each relative to its own start-month and lead mean) and G oℓ that of the observed <ref type="bibr">Niño 3.4</ref> anomalies in the corresponding target months.

text.text: A member anomaly x j of the real-time forecast is mapped to with values beyond the range of the reference sample held at its extremes.

The observations are the monthly ERSST Niño 3.4 anomalies whose three-month running mean is the ONI the statistical models were fitted on, so the corrected forecast is on the scale of the fitted ENSO exposure-response.

The ensemble spread is then set to the error of the corrected ensemble mean in the same 1991-2020 sample, oℓ , where bars denote ensemble means, RMSE oℓ is the root mean squared error of the mapped ensemble mean against observations and σ 2  oℓ the mean raw ensemble variance.

We scale the raw member deviations rather than the mapped ones because, in an event outside the range of the reference sample, the range limit of (S26) maps all members to the same value and would remove the spread entirely; CPC avoids this with a larger real-time ensemble.
Only the calibrated ensemble mean is therefore held within the range of the reference sample; the members spread around it without a limit.

Mapped instead to OISST v2.1 observations [64], this procedure reproduces CPC's own corrected ensemble means for the January to June 2026 forecasts to within 0.05-0.13 °C at leads of 0 to 6 months, where CPC's correction itself moves the forecast by 0.2-0.7 °C. For the forecast issued on 8 October 2026, the ERSST-calibrated seasonal means are within 0.08 °C (root mean squared difference) of CPC's corrected forecast from October-December 2026 to April-June 2027, whereas the raw forecast exceeds it by up to 0.8 °C.
text.formatted: Mapped instead to OISST v2.1 observations <ref type="bibr">[64]</ref>, this procedure reproduces CPC's own corrected ensemble means for the January to June 2026 forecasts to within 0.05-0.13 °C at leads of 0 to 6 months, where CPC's correction itself moves the forecast by 0.2-0.7 °C. For the forecast issued on 8 October 2026, the ERSST-calibrated seasonal means are within 0.08 °C (root mean squared difference) of CPC's corrected forecast from October-December 2026 to April-June 2027, whereas the raw forecast exceeds it by up to 0.8 °C.

text.text: We join the calibrated members to the observed record.

Months already observed take the monthly ERSST value; the CFSv2 analysis months that precede the first forecast month are used only where the monthly ERSST record has not yet been released, after shifting them so that the three-month mean of the latest published ONI season is reproduced.
The ONI of each trajectory is computed as a three-month running mean, using the published ONI wherever available.
In the forward simulations, the ONI entering a model is clamped to an interval around its boundary knots.

With lo and hi the lower and upper boundary knots of the model's ENSO basis (the observed ONI range of its group) and ϵ the clamp margin, the ONI is held within [lo -ϵ |lo|, hi + ϵ |hi|], with ϵ = 0.25 in the forecast, counterfactual, hindcast and past-event arms and in the analytic cross-check.
Within this interval the natural spline extrapolates linearly beyond the knots; outside it the effect is held at its value at the interval bound.
The calibrated forecast of the 2026-27 El Niño reaches or exceeds the upper knot of several fitted curves, where an unbounded extrapolation would be unsupported by the data.
ENSO phases follow one rule set.

The NOAA CPC episode rule (ONI at or beyond ±0.5 °C for at least five consecutive overlapping three-month seasons) is used for the ENSO-state shading of the figures and for the summary of the reconstruction by phase.
The cholera-year state of an outbreak and the classification of analogue winters use a threshold phase at ±0.5 °C without a persistence requirement.
The launch of a past event requires the ONI to stay beyond ±0.5 °C from the month after the launch to the event's first peak (Section S1.6.16).

Fig.S1.

Analysis workflow. (a) Data preparation: sub-national surveillance records, complemented by WHO national data (1), give outbreaks (2) that are mapped to administrative units (3) and consolidated into one episode per unit and cholera year (4), forming the occurrence, duration and monthly case-count datasets (5); ENSO is measured by the Oceanic Niño Index at lags of -11 to +11 months (6). (b) Statistical models: a latent-class model partitions the countries into five ENSO groups (7); hierarchical Bayesian models are fitted for each group and analysis(8), at lags selected by cross-validation (9), giving exposure-response curves(10). (c) Simulation: a particle filter reconstructs the outbreak state of every unit up to August 2026(11); forecast and counterfactual ENSO inputs (12) drive forward simulations (13), whose difference gives the outbreak burden attributable to ENSO(14).
